entries.title: Jesse White Tumbling Team eliminated from ‘America’s Got Talent’
entries.summary: <p>The Jesse White Tumbling Team’s journey on Season 21 of “America’s Got Talent” ended on Wednesday night as the Chicago troupe did not advance to the semifinal rounds of the hit reality/competition series. The outcome was revealed during the show’s first results round telecast.</p><p>The team's disappointment was palpable as their hopeful smiles dissolved into heartbreak as the news was announced.</p><p>Viewer votes, based on the previous night’s live quarterfinals performances, determined the three acts (out of 11) that would advance to the next phase of competition — the semifinals scheduled for Sept. 15.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/08/17/jesse-white-tumbling-team-americas-got-talent" target="_blank" >Jesse White Tumbling Team gets second chance on ‘America’s Got Talent’ as troupe rolls into live rounds </a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/6OMWRQEDz1Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Jesse White Tumbling Team Brings the HEAT With 92-Year-Old Jesse White | Quarterfinals | AGT 2026"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Earlier in the evening, the Tumblers were among the top five vote-getting acts overall, which also included Olivia Befus and her trained dog act; rapper Luke Taleno; light-up dance trio Royal Lasers; and comedian Cris Sosa. Befus, Taleno and Royal Lasers earned the round's three spots in the semifinals based on viewer vote totals.</p><p>Four additional “golden buzzer” acts — one from each of the four quarterfinal rounds, and determined by judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Sofia Vergara and Howie Mandel — are automatically propelled to the show's finals on Sept. 22. South Korean magic act Hundred Fingers earned the coveted buzzer on Tuesday night from Mandel.</p><p>The tumblers exhibited their time-tested winning form <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6OMWRQEDz1Q" target="_blank" >during their quarterfinals set </a> on Tuesday night, performing to the pulsating rhythms of Jamiroquai’s “Canned Heat."</p><p>Utilizing two across-stage runs of gymnastic mats, the team flew in and out at a frenetic pace — rolling, jumping, somersaulting and flying through the air, at one point even towering up and over the organization’s 92-year-old founder, Jesse White.</p><p>Cowell praised the performance, commenting: “Well, I loved your first audition, and then I was thinking, Can they make it better on the live shows? Can I be honest? It was better.”</p><p>South Korean K-pop boy band NCT 127 opened the results show on Wednesday night ahead of the group’s upcoming album, "BLINGY," releasing Aug. 24.</p><p>Vergara later took a moment during the telecast to remind viewers of the recent devastating earthquake in Colombia, asking viewers to support UNICEF and World Central Kitchen in their ongoing aid efforts in the region.</p><p>“AGT” fans will be voting for additional semifinalists from three more live quarterfinal rounds airing at 7 p.m. Aug. 25, Sept. 1 and Sept. 8 on NBC.</p><p><i>Miriam Di Nunzio is the former Features Editor of the Chicago Sun-Times.</i></p>
entries.author: Miriam Di Nunzio

entries.title: Court order gives players under pro contracts a chance to return to college sports
entries.summary: <p>Several athletes, including some who signed contracts with NFL teams, were granted a temporary restraining order by a Louisiana court that would make them eligible to return to college athletics, ESPN reported Wednesday.</p><p>Former Oregon State running back Anthony Hankerson (Seattle Seahawks), former Florida and LSU pass rusher Jack Pyburn (Tampa Bay Buccaneers) and ex-Mississippi starters Dae'Quan Wright (Cleveland Browns) and Wydett Williams (Arizona Cardinals) are on NFL rosters and were part of the lawsuit.</p><p>NFL teams are deep into training camp, and rosters have to be cut to 53 players by Aug. 30. Many who don't make those clubs could look for a fallback plan in college football, barring a successful appeal by the NCAA.</p><p>According to ESPN, 16 football players were part of the lawsuit that included 33 athletes across several sports who are seeking a fifth year of eligibility.</p><p>The NCAA has been dealt a series of legal setbacks regarding its eligibility rules.</p><p>"Courts across the country granting relief to ineligible athletes who already had every opportunity to compete in college — sometimes without even having a hearing — are failing to appreciate the destabilizing effect their rulings are having on college sports," Tim Buckley, NCAA senior vice president of external affairs, said in a statement.</p><p>"The lawyers bringing these cases seemingly won't be satisfied until every professional athlete can treat college sports as a fallback option, regardless of the opportunities it strips from those who will never have a chance to begin their collegiate sports experience."</p><p>On July 31, a federal court in Denver ruled that all high school class of 2022 athletes who exhausted their fourth season of college eligibility this spring are eligible for a fifth season this academic year.</p><p>That decision came a little more than a month after the NCAA passed a rule that gives athletes five years to complete five seasons of competition, starting with those who enroll in the fall of 2027. The Colorado ruling eliminated the waiting period.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Private school advantage? Batavia's Piron, Mount Carmel's Lynch sound off as the IHSA debates changes
entries.summary: <p>Batavia coach Dennis Piron and Mount Carmel coach Jordan Lynch represent opposite ends of the spectrum in the state’s ongoing debate over whether or not private schools currently have an advantage in high school football.</p><p>Their teams matched up in super-charged playoff games over the past several years, and the two rabid fanbases have built a rivalry that might not be entirely healthy. But both coaches are engaging and pleasant and make well-thought out, solid points when they give their opinions on the state’s rules.</p><p>High school sports success tends to have cycles. Private schools are currently riding high on the state’s football scene. The preseason rankings reflect that, as all of the top five schools are Catholic League powers.</p><p>Private schools won all eight of the Class 8A and Class 7A state championships over the past four seasons. Private schools took home 18 of the 25 state titles awarded in Class 4A through 8A since COVID canceled the 2020 season.</p><p>“I’ve been doing this a long time,” Piron said. “The private schools have always been able to attract kids to their schools based on the quality of their programs. I have no problem with that.</p><p>“But in the last 10 years, it feels a little bit more like they are an IMG or a prep school than just a private school. I’ve always thought the Mount Carmel and Loyola’s of the world were tough to beat. And now you have kids announcing things on social media that they are moving from Wisconsin, and you see all the distances they are traveling to private schools. The [private school] coaches are clearly coming out and saying they recruit. That is different.”</p><p>Illinois High School Association rules allow private schools to enroll players within a 30-mile radius.</p><p>Lynch has pointed out multiple times that Mount Carmel’s location actually limits its radius more than 30 miles: “We can’t go in the lake and grab kids.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/19/michael-obrien-preseason-super-25-high-school-football-rankings" >Michael O’Brien’s preseason Super 25 high school football rankings</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/18/mount-carmel-football-chicago-ihsa" >Top-ranked Mount Carmel reloads for five-peat with 19 future college players</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/10/batavia-football-ihsa" >‘Get your popcorn ready’ because it is state title or bust for No. 8 Batavia</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lynch hasn’t acted differently than private school programs of the past, but he is more willing to advocate for private school recruiting. And he isn’t going to apologize for Mount Carmel’s success. The Caravan have won four consecutive state titles and are heavily favored to win Class 8A again this season. Their roster features 19 players with college scholarship offers. </p><p>“Give the kids and the families some credit, that are traveling within the 30 miles,” Lynch said. “It isn’t easy for them. They have to wake up every Monday, Wednesday, Friday in the offseason and be here at 5:30 a.m. No one sees that; no one talks about that. We have too many critics out there instead of people encouraging these kids and patting them on the back for doing some uncommon things.”</p><p>Mount Carmel doesn’t hide where its players live. The school distributes a media guide which lists the hometowns of every player on the varsity roster. This year’s Caravan is made up of 55 Chicagoans, 17 players from the south suburbs, five players from Indiana and one player each from Skokie, Park Ridge, North Aurora and Lisle.</p><p>“These kids and these parents have a choice,” Lynch said. “For them to pass up a school in their district and come to Mount Carmel and pay tuition speaks volumes. And I think you need to check your own programs. Why are kids passing up your school? They have a choice. They see what is going on here. These kids are pushed every single day. They work hard and we hold them accountable.”</p><p>Boys basketball, the state’s other high-profile sport with a significant fanbase, hasn’t seen such a significant swing towards private school success. Public schools have won 11 titles since COVID with private schools winning nine.</p><p>The IHSA’s competitive balance committee debated the private school dominance issue in mid-July. One proposal discussed creating separate playoff paths for public and private schools, with seven public schools and one private school advancing to the Elite Eight in sports with playoff brackets.</p><p>That’s a drastic step, but certainly better than the prospect of splitting the state tournaments into two, with one for public schools and one for private schools.</p><p>Expect several public schools to propose a change to the 30-mile recruiting radius this winter when the IHSA votes on new bylaws. The issue isn’t going away any time soon.</p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Federal disaster loan centers to open for second time in 2 months following late July storms
entries.summary: <p>For the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/feds-to-open-disaster-loan-application-help-centers-in-wake-of-june-storms" target="_blank" ><u>second time this year</u></a>, the U.S. Small Business Administration plans to open Disaster Loan Outreach Centers for people affected by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/27/weather-storms-heat-wind" target="_blank" ><u>severe storms</u></a> that ravaged large swaths of Northern Illinois late last month.</p><p>The centers are set to open in Chicago Thursday and in suburban Hazel Crest Friday. The Chicago location will be open until Sept. 3, and the suburban location until Sept. 4.</p><p>They will have representatives to answer questions about the loan program, explain the application process and help to make applications for residents who saw damage from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" ><u>July 27 storms</u></a>. Walk-ins will be accepted, and appointments can be made <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/appointment.sba.gov/__;!!B24N9PvjPQId!Yui7iQbfqrrUKv8IM-98BdLyEdY4caVYvQlLo-hfOfnfkOUBI4UKHY9fTWrFsPblrWUdvM_M9Bs0tZJjcknmMRbMCkoTxQ$" target="_blank" ><u>online</u></a>.</p><p>Homeowners and renters can apply for as much as $100,000 to repair or replace damaged or destroyed personal property like appliances and furniture. Applications are also open for up to $500,000 in low-interest loans to repair or replace real estate damaged or destroyed during the storms.</p><p>Businesses and nonprofits can apply to borrow up to $2 million for damages.</p><p>The deadline to apply for physical property damage is Oct. 19, though economic injury applications aren’t due until May 18, 2027.</p><p>The nearest office and its hours can be found on the U.S. Small Business Administration’s <a class="Link" href="https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/appointment.sba.gov/__;!!B24N9PvjPQId!Yui7iQbfqrrUKv8IM-98BdLyEdY4caVYvQlLo-hfOfnfkOUBI4UKHY9fTWrFsPblrWUdvM_M9Bs0tZJjcknmMRbMCkoTxQ$" target="_blank" ><u>website</u></a>.</p><p>The Chicago Public Library’s Pullman branch will serve as the Chicago location. It will be open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Mondays and Wednesdays, noon to 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.</p><p>The suburban site will be at the Village of Hazel Crest’s building, 3601 W. 183rd St. It will be open 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday, and 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.</p><p>The federal agency <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/feds-to-open-disaster-loan-application-help-centers-in-wake-of-june-storms" target="_blank" ><u>opened outreach centers last month</u></a> following a series of three storms <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/11/obstruction-on-tracks-causes-service-disruption-on-cta-yellow-line-trains-after-storms" target="_blank" ><u>June 10</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/12/chicago-severe-weather-tornadoes-power-outage-comed-customers-englewood" target="_blank" ><u>June 11</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/16/storms-to-bring-torrential-rainfall-potential-flooding-tornadoes-to-chicago-area-wednesday" target="_blank" ><u>June 17</u></a>, which also prompted Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/pritzker-disaster-proclamation-tornado-flood" target="_blank" ><u>issue a disaster proclamation</u></a>.</p><p>Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" target="_blank" ><u>signed another disaster proclamation</u></a> Tuesday for the July 27 storms.</p><p>Earlier Wednesday afternoon, the Cook County Board of Review also urged residents to document any damage to their homes that occurred during severe weather this year, as they could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/19/cook-county-board-of-review-urges-residents-to-start-on-appeals-for-2026-tax-bills-after-recent-storm-damage" target="_blank" ><u>potentially be eligible for reductions on their tax bills</u></a> if the damage meets the county’s qualifications.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/19/cook-county-board-of-review-urges-residents-to-start-on-appeals-for-2026-tax-bills-after-recent-storm-damage" >Cook County Board of Review urges residents to start appeals for 2026 tax bills after recent storm damage</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" >Pritzker signs disaster proclamation to aid recovery after months of ‘relentless and unprecedented’ storms</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Hundreds rally for 'union power' in support of Shedd workers contract fight
entries.summary: <p>Union workers from across the country flooded the lawn outside the Shedd Aquarium Wednesday in support of its union’s fight for a contract.</p><p>Several hundred union members, in town for the national conference of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, chanted and cheered as speakers riled up the crowd demanding Shedd management agree to a contract with better pay and benefits for the Shedd Workers United union.</p><p>Shedd workers moved to form a union in 2024 as part of a larger trend of workers at some of Chicago’s most iconic cultural institutions doing the same.</p><p>Several speakers referenced the fight to be recognized as a union, saying they’ve been fighting for their rights as workers for years as the Shedd has invested in “union busting lawyers” instead of fair wages for union members.</p><p>Union members wore bright green AFSCME shirts and held signs reading “solidarity” and “union power” as chants pulsed through the crowd against the backdrop of the Chicago skyline and Lake Michigan.</p><p>Lee Saunders, president of AFSCME national and Shedd workers, said Shedd's proposals were insulting.</p><p>“They said no, they didn’t want to give you wage increases,” Saunders said. “They didn’t want to give you what you’re due.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: 1 man killed, another critically wounded in McKinley Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>One man was killed and another seriously injured during a shooting in the McKinley Park neighborhood Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The two men, 26 and 56, were inside a van in the 3800 block of South Western Boulevard at 3:51 p.m. when several people got out of a nearby Honda and fired shots, police said. </p><p>The younger man was shot multiple times and taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital where he later died.</p><p>The elder man was shot in the torso and also taken to the same hospital where he was listed in critical condition, police said.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Lewandowski's penalty kick proves to be the winner for Fire
entries.summary: <p>Robert Lewandowski scored on a penalty kick, Puso Dithejane added a goal, and the Chicago Fire beat Orlando City 2-1 on Wednesday in Orlando, Florida, in a game delayed about 90 minutes by inclement weather.</p><p>The Fire (11-8-2) have won three in a row. Chris Brady had three saves for Chicago.</p><p>Lewandowski drew a penalty conceded by Robin Jansson and converted from the spot to cap the scoring in the 68th minute.</p><p>Dithejane scored from just inside the top of the box to give the Fire a 1-0 lead in the fourth minute.</p><p>David Brekalo redirected a corner kick played in by Antoine Griezmann in the 52nd for Orlando City (6-11-3).</p><p>The game was paused in the 44th minute due to lightning in the area.<br></p>

entries.title: Motorcyclist killed in Loop collision with car, 1 in custody
entries.summary: <p>The 25-year-old driver of a car that hit and killed a woman riding a motorcycle was arrested after the late Wednesday crash in the Loop. </p><p>Charges are pending but have been announced by police early Thursday. </p><p>The crash happened around 11:30 p.m. in the 400 block of South DuSable Lake Shore Drive as the southbound car crashed into the motorcycle, which was also southbound. </p><p>The motorcyclist, a 49-year-old woman, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where she died, police said. Her name has not been released.</p>

entries.title: Bears' secondary doesn't look ready for NFC North loaded with powerful pass catchers
entries.summary: <p>The NFC North has long been known as the NFL’s most bruising, old-school division, and it does trend that way when winter hits, but battles between <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> and their rivals have increasingly gone to the air.</p><p>The Bears don’t look ready for that at the moment.</p><p>Their secondary, once a roster strength, is dicey as they head into what should be a wide-open division race. The Lions and Packers have prolific quarterbacks in Jared Goff and Jordan Love, respectively, and the Vikings are trying to relaunch two-time Pro Bowl selection Kyler Murray.</p><p>Each of those teams is stacked with pass catchers, and that’s where concerns rise for the Bears.</p><p>They still have an elite shutdown cornerback in Jaylon Johnson, assuming he truly is back to normal after a major injury derailed him last season, but that’s not enough. He negates one threat, theoretically, and the North teams bring much more to the table than that.</p><p>The Bears’ secondary already had uncertainty as they started over at safety and made no big moves at cornerback. Then their key offseason pickup, Super Bowl champion safety Coby Bryant, went down with a potentially season-ending knee injury.</p><p>That leaves a lot of responsibility on rookie Dillion Thieneman.</p><p>Ever-unpredictable cornerback Tyrique Stevenson has been out with a minor injury and missed practice again Wednesday. He usually has had to fight off Terell Smith to keep his starting spot, but Smith is out, too.</p><p>And then there’s the odd and maddening saga of nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, who in one year has gone from one of the surest things on the roster to a total question mark. He missed 14 games last season because of three separate injuries, then suffered another one in the offseason and has yet to practice.</p><p>Asking about it doesn’t go over well at Halas Hall.</p><p>Bears coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> was prodded for an update Saturday and said only, “Unknown.” Pressed again a couple days later for even the most general information about what’s going on, he gave four consecutive short answers.</p><p>That series ended with a basic inquiry of what exactly Gordon does every day, to which Johnson replied, “He’s rehabbing,” then looked for the next question.</p><p>Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen was “hopeful” Wednesday that Gordon would be back soon, but regarding the chances of him playing in the season opener against the Panthers, he said, “That's something I can’t put a lot of thought into right now.”</p><p>Allen will have his hands full matching up with North offenses even at full strength:</p><p>- The Packers have wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, each of whom did damage against the Bears last season, plus ascending tight end Tucker Kraft.</p><p>- The Lions have the most firepower with two 1,000-yard wide receivers in Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, former Pro Bowl tight end Sam LaPorta and running back Jahmyr Gibbs, who was third at his position last season with 77 catches.</p><p>- It’s easy to brush aside the Vikings after a down season, but coach Kevin O’Connell has made it work with quarterbacks far less talented than Murray. And he’ll be throwing to overwhelming wide receiver Justin Jefferson, two of the best complementary receivers in Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings and two-time Pro Bowl tight end T.J. Hockenson.</p><p>Who’s going to cover all those guys?</p><p>The Bears will be in trouble if they can’t answer that.</p><p>Even while going 11-6 and winning the North comfortably last season, they went 2-4 in the division and allowed an average of 223.5 yards passing and a 103 passer rating in those games.</p><p>Jaylon Johnson said a few weeks ago the notion of trying to win 40-35 every week is “unacceptable.” It’s probably impossible.</p><p>There aren’t obvious solutions to this problem, but it’s on Allen to unearth them. Otherwise, another season of shaky defense could undermine any progress the Bears make offensively.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: ICE intimidated, then admitted it targeted man just for his negative critique
entries.summary: <p>Last June, two investigators employed by the Department of Homeland Security showed up at David Streever's house in Rochester, New York. Streever was not home, so they left him a note.</p><p>That <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.2.pdf" target="_blank" >note</a>, presented as an official warning from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, is at the center of a First Amendment <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.0.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> that Streever <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/07/he-compared-ices-chief-to-a-nazi-so-ice-tracked-him-down-on-vacation-with-his-daughter/" target="_blank" >filed</a> last month, alleging that ICE agents investigated and threatened him based on his constitutionally protected criticism of their boss. This month, the government <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/17/nx-s1-5934692/dhs-free-speech-investigations" target="_blank" >responded</a> to Streever's lawsuit, confirming his allegations while attempting to rebut them.</p><p>On Jan. 26, two days after DHS agents <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/25/dhs-again-promises-a-thorough-investigation-of-a-fatal-shooting-after-prejudging-the-outcome/" target="_blank" >fatally shot</a> Minneapolis protester Alex Pretti, Streever sent an angry <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.1_1.pdf" target="_blank" >email</a> to Todd Lyons, then the acting ICE director. Streever called Lyons "a monstrous human being," likened him to the genocidal Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich, and predicted that he would be haunted by "shame at your own pathetic weakness" in defending the Pretti shooting "until your last day on Earth."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Streever's evaluation of Lyons was harsh, to say the least. But he did not say anything that could reasonably be construed as a threat of violence.</p><p>Brent Goodwin, assistant director for investigations at ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, nevertheless claims Streever's email "had potential threatening undertones" and "potentially present[ed] a safety concern." </p><p>Because "ICE OPR did not have any information about Mr. Streever when the email came in," Goodwin says in an Aug. 5 <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.20.1.pdf" target="_blank" >declaration</a>, it "determined that it needed to conduct an ICE investigation."</p><p>What happened next makes little sense if ICE's investigators, who did not even try to contact Streever until five months after his email, were attempting to resolve a legitimate "safety concern." But their actions are completely understandable if they were trying to intimidate an ICE critic.</p><p>"YOU MAY BE IN VIOLATION OF FEDERAL LAW," said the "<a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.2.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>WARNING NOTICE</u></a><u>"</u> that two agents left with Streever's wife in Rochester on June 23. It cited two statutes, one dealing with <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/115" target="_blank" >threats of violence</a> against federal officials, the other making it a crime to <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/119" target="_blank" >reveal</a> "restricted personal information" about them with the intent to intimidate or incite violence against them.</p><p>Streever had not violated either of those laws. But the notice said ICE had "reason to believe" his email to Lyons "may constitute a violation of Title 18 of the United States Code," which <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/event/113th-congress/house-event/LC21283/text?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >includes</a> more than 1,500 offenses.</p><p>The document asked Streever to "promptly remove and/or discontinue the aforementioned behavior." It added that "receipt of this Notice will be taken into consideration, should you continue to be involved in any criminal activities described above."</p><p>In addition to delivering the notice, DHS agents unsuccessfully tried to intercept Streever at John F. Kennedy International Airport when he returned from a trip to Finland with his 7-year-old daughter on June 25. They also repeatedly tried to contact him in person and by telephone at the New York hotel where he stayed that night.</p><p>After that, Goodwin says, ICE gave up, closing the case on June 30 because "all investigative leads" had been "exhausted." ICE did that even though its agents had never managed to interview Streever so they could determine "whether or not [he] presented a threat," which Goodwin describes as the object of the investigation.</p><p>Seeking dismissal of Streever's lawsuit, the government's lawyers <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.20.0.pdf" target="_blank" >concede</a> his email to Lyons "put words to his disagreements with a current administration official." In other words, they admit he was investigated because of speech protected by the First Amendment.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/15/ice-is-determined-to-unmask-a-reddit-user-whose-only-crime-seems-to-be-criticizing-ice/" target="_blank" >Other ICE critics</a> have received <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/06/29/ice-warns-syracuse-poll-worker-to-delete-a-political-instagram-post/" target="_blank" >similar treatment</a>. The Wall Street Journal <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/ice-surveillance-internet-critics-e3b22f49" target="_blank" >reports</a> that the agency "has deployed a round-the-clock digital dragnet" that tracks online speech to identify more targets.</p><p>ICE's retaliatory campaign, Streever's lawyers at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.22.0.pdf" target="_blank" >warn</a>, threatens the freedom to criticize police conduct without fear of arrest. Four decades ago, the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-482/pdf/USREPORTS-482-451.pdf" target="_blank" >described</a> that ability as "one of the principal characteristics by which we distinguish a free nation from a police state."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2a0000" name="module-2a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Critics Pan Senior's Repeat Performances
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am 70 and consider my mental faculties to be normal. One aging issue my wife and I have noticed is that I tend to repeat stories to our children, grandchildren and friends. Our children can be less than forgiving toward this old boomer as they deliver a comment like, "Yeah, we've already heard about that," sometimes in a rude or caustic tone.</p><p>We think this phenomenon is common to a lot of people our age. I have started prefacing my stories with "Did I tell you about ..." before talking. They could be nicer by saying early on in the story: "Yes, Dad, you've told that story. Is anything new?" What does Dear Abby think? — <i>RECOLLECTIONS ON REPEAT</i></p><p><b>DEAR RECOLLECTIONS:</b> I agree that your family and friends could be more polite when they point out that they've "heard this one before." However, if you find people are interrupting your "greatest hits" too often, it's time to mention it to your doctor.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My thoughtful staff bought me a Fitbit last Christmas. It's a generous gift, but I haven't used it, and I don't think I will. How do I tell them I appreciate the gift and their generosity but I just don't want it and won't wear it. They have already addressed the fact that they haven't seen it on my wrist. — <i>WON'T USE IT IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR WON'T USE IT:</b> Your staff must be devoted and wish you a long and healthy life. I find the fact that they gave you a Fitbit to be quite impressive. In fairness, I must warn you. If you put it on, I know from experience that you may find yourself immediately addicted. The way to handle this might actually be to give it a try and tell your employees that you are using it at home. It may prod you off your behind and into a healthier lifestyle.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I were together for 10 years, married for nine. He recently passed away at the age of 42. His death was unexpected, and I was the one who found him. He'd had an epileptic seizure while home alone. I have serious anxiety driving home every day now.</p><p>I've been looking for grief counseling, support groups, etc., but there seems to be a recurring theme: Young widows and widowers (under 50) are underserved. I don't mean to diminish anyone else's grief, but at the same time, I do not want to hear "We had a great long life together" from a much older woman when my experience has been nothing like hers. Members of the younger generation need different support, and it just isn't there. — <i>YOUNG AND GRIEVING</i></p><p><b>DEAR YOUNG AND GRIEVING:</b> Please allow me to offer my deepest sympathy. Losing your husband at such an early age must have been a terrible shock. It's not surprising that you have trouble relating to people whose loss happened much later in life.</p><p>For a support group geared toward younger people, you might have better luck online. Search for "young widow support group," and you will find chat forums and video meetups as well as resources to help you rebuild your life. It's not the same as meeting face-to-face, but it may help.</p>

entries.title: ‘Dance for Life’ puts the spotlight on healthcare gaps for Chicago performers
entries.summary: <p>Contemporary ballet dancer Nia Davis is in demand.</p><p>Beyond performing with <a class="Link" href="https://www.visceraldance.com/" target="_blank" >Visceral Dance Chicago</a>, she also teaches at the company and at another studio in the suburbs.</p><p>But juggling multiple jobs, often for financial reasons, sometimes takes a toll on her body.</p><p>“I remember getting so sick because I was like, ‘I’ve got to make money,’” said Davis, of Humboldt Park. “And my health started to deplete.”</p><p>Earlier this year, Davis sustained fractures in her foot that she was able to get treated quickly as a dependent on her parents’ insurance. But when she turns 26 in November, she’ll have to figure out another plan for coverage, which is not provided by her employers.</p><p>“I have no idea,” she said of her next steps. “Hopefully it comes to me with ease.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e50000" name="image-e50000"></a> </figure> </div> </div><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdhf.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Dance Health Fund</a> addresses needs for dancers like Davis by providing dozens of healthcare grants each year. And on Saturday at The Auditorium, it will host its 35th “<a class="Link" href="https://www.cdhf.org/danceforlife" target="_blank" >Dance for Life</a>” fundraiser, a nearly sold-out show that will highlight 11 local dance companies and the works of notable choreographers, including a world-premiere finale by Ryan Duncan. The event is on track to raise $500,000.</p><p>The nonprofit has seen an increase in grant applications in recent years, as many dancers are uninsured or underinsured. And the industry’s prominent union for dancers, <a class="Link" href="https://www.musicalartists.org/" target="_blank" >American Guild of Musical Artists</a>, has seen an uptick in organizing among dancers. Leaders at both organizations say the demand for assistance is only going to escalate as underfunded, financially strapped arts organizations struggle to keep up with rising healthcare costs.</p><p>“Healthcare is a problem the nation has to solve, and what we're doing now is filling in the gaps in the dam before it collapses from the leaks,” said James Odom, a regional director of the union, which represents about 100 dancers in the Chicago area, including members of the Joffrey Ballet. “That's not sustainable.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bd0000" name="module-bd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>‘Dance For Life’</b></h3><br><b>When:</b> Aug. 22, 7:30 p.m.<br><b>Where:</b> The Auditorium, 50 E. Ida B. Wells Dr.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $75+ at <a class="Link" href="http://auditoriumtheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>auditoriumtheatre.org</u></a></div> </div><p>Before assisting dancers with general healthcare needs, “Dance for Life” began as a benefit for AIDS Foundation Chicago during the height of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. While the Chicago Dance Health Fund still donates to the foundation, it has expanded its focus to offer $5,000 Critical Health Needs Grants and $1,000 General Health and Wellness Grants. Dancers have used the money for everything from cancer treatments and hip replacements to dental visits and physical therapy.</p><p>The dance fund also partners with health organizations such as Howard Brown Health, Athletico Physical Therapy, Shirley Ryan AbilityLab and the American Cancer Society to offer dancers free or discounted care.</p><p>While some dance companies like Joffrey Ballet and Deeply Rooted Dance Theater provide insurance plans, many can’t afford to, especially if they have limited seasons of programming. As a result, some dancers seek coverage through the Affordable Care Act. But they often have to balance working enough jobs to pay their bills, while still qualifying for Medicaid or lower premiums.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>Dancers who have contracts with the Lyric Opera of Chicago, Chicago Opera Theater, Chicago Symphony Chorus and the Grant Park Chorus have access to some healthcare assistance, retirement funds or other benefits through the American Guild of Musical Artists. But some of those allowances have been limited by complicated federal regulations in recent years, Odom said.</p><p>“Running an arts organization is difficult,” said Michael Anderson, managing advisor of the Chicago Dance Health Fund. “Some of the smaller companies really do look to us for some help with dancers, especially if they get injured and need rehabilitation.”</p><p>It’s a relief for dancers, who sometimes downplay their injuries out of fear of exorbitant medical bills, Davis said. entries.title: As Trump pushes sweeping changes to mail voting, here's where things stand in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>As President Donald Trump continues to challenge mail ballots and push for a nationwide eligible registry list, many voters are confused about their own rights in the November midterm elections.</p><p>Trump in late July asked the U.S. Supreme Court to halt lower court decisions that blocked a March executive order that would have made the federal government create a list of eligible voters and then make the U.S. Postal Service deliver mail ballots specifically to those on the list. Trump also wants the federal government to investigate and prosecute officials who issue ballots to “noncitizens.” The executive order came amid the president’s claims that people who lack legal status are voting.</p><p>Trump also is pushing Congress to pass his proposed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, dubbed the SAVE Act, which would require proof of citizenship to vote. But his efforts have repeatedly stalled in the Senate.</p><p>Despite his ongoing fight against mail-in voting. Trump voted by mail once again in Florida's Republican primary. He also voted by mail in a special election in Palm Beach County earlier this year.</p><p>In Illinois, “There’s really nothing that’s changed yet,” State Board of Elections spokeswoman Bernadette Matthews said. “It’s business as usual with operations and Illinois law that runs alongside federal requirements. Nothing has been changed from previous cycles right now through any of the federal actions or the litigation yet.”</p><p>Here’s where things stand 10 weeks before Election Day.</p><h3><b>Can I vote if I live abroad?</b></h3><p>Illinois citizens who live overseas or are serving in the U.S. armed forces can register and vote by mail. Military personnel are allowed to register to vote and apply for a vote-by-mail ballot at the same time under Illinois law. The Federal Post Card Application is provided by the Department of Defense to let members of the armed forces, their dependents and U.S. citizens abroad to vote by mail and, if necessary, to register to vote.</p><h3><b>Can I view my voter registration information online?</b></h3><p>Yes. The Illinois State Board of Elections has a <a class="Link" href="https://ova.elections.il.gov/RegistrationLookup.aspx" target="_blank" ><u>registration website</u></a> where you can look up your registry with simple information like your full name, date of birth, address and Zip code. It also gives you the deadlines to register. Applications are now open to request a vote-by-mail ballot in Illinois, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/vote-mail#cboe-vote-by-mail" target="_blank" >online application for those in Chicago.</a> All requests by mail must be made by Sept. 24. Voters also can request a mail ballot in person.</p><h3><b>Do I need a passport to prove I’m a citizen to vote?</b></h3><p>No. In Illinois, you need at least one form of ID that has your current address to be able to register to vote — but not to actually vote. That could include a driver's license, bank statement, lease, utility bill or state ID. The SAVE Act would require a passport, a certified birth certificate with a photo ID, a naturalization certificate or a Consular Report of Birth abroad to register to vote in person.</p><h3><b>Have people who lack legal status voted in Illinois?</b></h3><p>“Noncitizen” voting is extremely rare, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections. Since 1982, only 10 noncitizens have been confirmed to have voted in an Illinois election.</p><h3><b>What happens if someone lacking legal status tries to vote?</b></h3><p>Under the National Voter Registration Act, voters are not required to show proof of U.S. citizenship when they register to vote. Voters must attest, under penalty of perjury, that they are U.S. citizens when completing their voter registration applications.</p><p>Voter registration applications created by the Illinois State Board of Elections ask, “Are you a citizen of the United States?” Applicants also are required to certify the following: “The information I have provided is true to the best of my knowledge under penalty of perjury. If I have provided false information, then I may be fined, imprisoned, or, if I am not a U.S. citizen, deported from or refused entry into the United States.” </p><p>Voters who register by other methods must also attest to their status as a citizen. If an applicant does not make the required certification of citizenship, the voter registration application will be denied.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" name="image-8f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3c0304c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a96c6ec/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="People voting at George Rogers Clark Elementary School in Austin on March 17. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54fdf7c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70ad95f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2F03%2F535b05464d3e9c17cf76809d63f0%2Fprimaryvoters-260318-5-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>People voting at George Rogers Clark Elementary School in Austin on March 17.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Should I turn in my mail ballot early in light of U.S. Postal Service changes? </b></h3><p>Yes. The Illinois State Board of Elections is recommending that voters mail back ballots as early as possible. To ensure that your mail ballot will be counted, it must be postmarked by Election Day and be received by the board of elections no later than 14 days after the date of the election. Under a new policy, mail is postmarked on the day it is processed at the post office, rather than on the day it is dropped in a mailbox.</p><h3><b>Is a ballot drop box secure?</b></h3><p>Not every election authority in Illinois has one, but, yes, according to the Illinois State Board of Elections, which has security measures in place for drop boxes. If your local election authority doesn’t have a drop box, you can hand-deliver your vote-by-mail ballot directly to election authorities.</p><h3><b>What happens if I didn’t get my mail ballot or I got it but want to vote in person instead?</b></h3><p>If you didn’t receive the mail ballot, you can go to your local election authority, fill out an affidavit attesting to the non-receipt and vote with a regular ballot. If you got one and decided not to use it, you can surrender the vote-by-mail ballot to the election authority and then vote in person<b>. </b></p><h3><b>Do I need a REAL ID or a Social Security card to vote?</b></h3><p>No. You do not need to bring a REAL ID or a Social Security card to vote.</p><h3><b>Do I need to have the name on my birth certificate as my voter registration name?</b></h3><p>No. But Trump’s SAVE Act would require you to bring in additional paperwork, such as a marriage certificate, if your name doesn’t match other IDs that you’ve brought. According to the nonpartisan website <a class="Link" href="http://vote.org" target="_blank" ><u>Vote.org</u></a>, an estimated 69 million American women do not have a birth certificate that matches their current legal name.</p><h3><b>Does the Justice Department have access to the Illinois voter registration database?</b></h3><p>No. But the Trump administration is trying to make that happen. The Illinois State Board of Elections is keeping track of the latest court case, which has seen a federal judge rule against giving that access. So far, there has been no appeal of that ruling.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/03/donald-trump-executive-order-national-voter-eligibility-list-mail-in-ballots-lawsuit-24-blue-states" >Illinois and other Democrat-led states sue against Trump executive order that tightens mail-in voting</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Back-to-school supplies expected to be higher. How much would some CPS families spend?
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools students will head back to class next week with backpacks full of new supplies, mostly requested by their school.</p><p>School supply lists can have families spending more than previous years, but with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/06/11/spiking-gas-prices-chicagoans-stop-rising-food-prices-inflation" >rising inflation</a> some parents could be spending even more than they expected.</p><p>A Deloitte survey of Chicago K-12 parents found they planned to spend $794 per child on back-to-school items this year, up 7% year over year.</p><p>And rising costs could contribute to the figure. A report last month from Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation found the price of typical school supplies increased by 7.7% over the past year. The average price of some items saw sharp increases year over year, like lunch boxes, which jumped by 26.8%, notebooks (up 23%) and index cards (22.2%), according to the report.</p><p>CPS parent Karen Mannerino remembers spending less than $100 on school supplies for all three of her kids.</p><p>Now, as two kids head into second and fifth grade at Wildwood Elementary and the oldest starts 11th grade at Lane Tech College Prep, she estimates spending about $300 total to complete each child's supply list.</p><p>Mannerino said she started shopping in June and continued buying throughout the summer. In prior years, she purchased a box with the required school supplies sold by Wildwood. The box this year was $125 per kid.</p><p>“This year, I just felt like the box price was so much that I could probably get it cheaper if I bought it on my own,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" We managed to find items for the list totaling $57.83.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-840000" name="html-embed-module-840000"></a><iframe src="https://embed.documentcloud.org/documents/28565929-school-supplies-receipt-illustration-sixth-grade-walt-disney-magnet-school/?embed=1&title=0&onlyshoworg=1" width="172.5" height="348.42" style="border: 1px solid #d8dee2; border-radius: 0.5rem; width: 100%; height: 100%; max-width: 35rem; aspect-ratio: 172.5 / 410;" allow="fullscreen"></iframe> <p style="color: #666; font-size: 1rem;">Illustration: Justin Myers/​Chicago Public Media</p> </div> </div><p>Shopping for a kindergartner at Edwards Elementary in Archer Heights brought us to a total of $100.24. border-radius: 0.5rem; width: 100%; height: 100%; max-width: 35rem; aspect-ratio: 172.5 / 410;" allow="fullscreen"></iframe> <p style="color: #666; font-size: 1rem;">Illustration: Justin Myers/​Chicago Public Media</p> </div> </div><p>Using a ninth grade Morgan Park High School list, we rounded up an order that included eight plastic folders, graph paper and a Texas Instruments graphing calculator for a total of $141.13.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ec0000" name="html-embed-module-ec0000"></a><iframe src="https://embed.documentcloud.org/documents/28565927-school-supplies-receipt-illustration-ninth-grade-morgan-park-high-school/?embed=1&title=0&onlyshoworg=1" width="172.5" height="348.42" style="border: 1px solid #d8dee2; border-radius: 0.5rem; width: 100%; height: 100%; max-width: 35rem; aspect-ratio: 172.5 / 410;" allow="fullscreen"></iframe> <p style="color: #666; font-size: 1rem;">Illustration: Justin Myers/​Chicago Public Media</p> </div> </div><p>But these supply costs exclude school fees that many CPS parents are required to pay. </p><p>Mannerino’s high schooler has a $585 annual fee, and the fees for her younger kids are about $150 each.</p><p>There's also back-to-school clothes, shoes and accessories, which Deloitte estimates will take up a family's total school spending by about 54%.</p><p>But the economic uncertainty over the last year seems to have impacted consumer back to school shopping behavior.</p><p>Discretionary spending during the back to school season dropped for all income levels, JLL retail researcher Keisha Virtue said. </p><p>“Last year, we saw this huge shift towards shopping early, and now, it's totally dispersed and ... [parents are] waiting until they have the money to spend,” Keisha Virtue, retail researcher at JLL, said. </p><p>Virtue said discretionary spending also dropped across all income levels, during this year's back-to-school shopping season. </p><p>The average parent is devoting 55.8% of their back-to-school budget to discretionary items, rather than necessities like for school supply lists. That's down from 60% last year. For households earning between $50,000 and $150,000, discretionary spending dropped from 64.9% in 2024 to 55.8% in 2026. Households earning more than $150,000 also dropped their discretionary spending from 70.9% to 57.1% over the same period, the sharpest decline at 13.8 percentage points.</p><p>Financial strain led shoppers to bargain hunt more than in past years, according to JLL research. </p><p>Dollar stores broke into the top 10 for back-to-school retailers for the first time. While Walmart has been a mainstay for back-to school-shopping, the retailer surged in popularity this year, by 22.5 percentage points, to 77.3%. The top three retailers were Walmart, Target and Amazon, according to JLL. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/08/08/chicago-parents-cps-outspend-us-average-back-to-school-supplies-survey" >Chicago parents expect to outspend U.S. average on back-to-school supplies, survey shows</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: No clear leader in race for Chicago school board president, poll finds
entries.summary: <p>A third of likely voters in November’s elections have no idea which of the five candidates for Chicago School Board president they’d vote for, or if they’d vote at all, according to a poll released Thursday that provides one of the first looks at the state of the historic contest.</p><p>The survey of 600 likely voters, which was commissioned by candidate Sendhil Revuluri’s campaign and conducted last week, found that even after hearing brief biographies about each candidate pulled from campaign materials, 34% of likely voters remained undecided or said they’d skip voting in the race.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/22/meet-the-candidates-for-chicagos-first-ever-elected-school-board-president" target="_blank" ><u>None of the five hopefuls</u></a> received overwhelming support. The poll found that 20% of likely voters would pick Hilario Dominguez, former political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, if the election were held today. Attorney Victor Henderson was next in line with support from 14% of likely voters.</p><p>Candidates who had experience serving on the board had the least support. Former board member Revuluri and sitting board member Jessica Biggs each got the backing of 11% of likely voters, while 9% said they’d vote for Jennifer Custer.</p><p>The findings indicate candidates still have work to do to distinguish themselves and that many voters are in the dark about a citywide race happening in less than three months. Though that isn’t a surprise because previous polls found <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/12/08/few-residents-know-chicago-will-have-a-fully-elected-school-board-poll-finds" target="_blank" ><u>few Chicago residents</u></a> were aware that voters will choose all 21 members of the Chicago School Board for the first time this fall.</p><p>Ethan Axelrod, of David Binder Research, which conducted the poll, said upwards of 80% of likely voters didn’t have an opinion on any of the candidates before they heard more about them. He said the survey shows Chicagoans are still getting to know the candidates and aren’t yet paying attention.</p><p>“They’re open to each of these candidates, really,” Axelrod said. “It’s a very fluid race.”</p><p>It’s also an expensive one. So far, most donations to school board candidates have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/16/spending-in-chicago-school-board-election-exceeds-1-6-million-as-limits-lift-in-race-for-board-president" target="_blank" ><u>poured into the president’s race.</u></a></p><p>The survey was conducted from Aug. 10 to 13 by phone and online and had a 4% margin of error.</p><p>Many likely voters seemed ready for a change. Six in 10 respondents said they disapproved of the job being done by the current school board.</p><p>And when presented with two approaches to address <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/12/cps-plans-cut-teacher-positions-raise-class-sizes-shrink-723-million-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>the district’s $732 million deficit</u></a>, just over half said they’d be more likely to vote for a candidate who can “make the hard calls,” while 36% said they’d choose someone who will “fight” for more state money, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>as the current board recently decided in an 11-7 vote</u></a>.</p><p>In one surprising finding, likely voters were nearly split on the issue of school closures.</p><p>Only 46% of respondents said they were more likely to vote for someone who is “strongly opposed” to closing and consolidating schools, while 42% said they would be less likely to support a candidate with that view.</p><p>The issue has frequently come up in campaign messaging given the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/chicagos-50-closed-schools" target="_blank" ><u>fallout from the district’s mass school closures in 2013</u></a>. Some candidates have come out strongly against closing schools <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2024/09/26/cps-board-votes-unanimously-prohibit-school-closures-until-2027" target="_blank" ><u>when a districtwide moratorium lifts</u></a>, or have tried to paint their opponents as advocates for closing schools.</p><p>“The fact that it’s as evenly divided as it is I think speaks to voters’ increasing awareness of the budget issues facing the district,” Axelrod said.</p>

and we are filling our fall itinerary with premieres: two world premieres — “The Birth of the Pill” at Timeline Theatre and “All the World” at Northlight Theatre — and one Chicago premiere of the Pulitzer Prize-winning play “A Strange Loop.”</p><p>Each performance will be followed by a panel conversation between WBEZ and the artists behind the show — and I will pass the mic to club members to pose a few questions, because we’re a community. We’ll conclude each event with a cocktail hour where we hang out, take pics and chat about all the plays we’ve seen around town.</p><p>And now the fun part. I get to announce this season’s slate of shows.</p><h3><b>Sept. 12: “</b><a class="Link" href="https://timelinetheatre.com/events/birth-pill/" target="_blank" ><b><u>The Birth of the Pill</u></b></a><b>” at TimeLine Theatre</b></h3><p>This world premiere written by Jessica Huang is based on the revelatory 2014 nonfiction book of the same title by Pulitzer Prize- winning Chicago author Jonathan Eig. The show is about a simple pill that will give women full control over their reproductive futures, and all of the obstacles in its development. This outing is a great opportunity to explore <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/04/03/in-uptown-timeline-theatre-moves-into-its-new-home-nearly-a-decade-in-the-making" target="_blank" ><u>TimeLine’s new building</u></a> in Edgewater and break in the new bar and lobby area after the show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ObD7Qjai55Y?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="A Strange Loop: Tiny Desk (Home) Concert"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Oct. 18: “</b><a class="Link" href="https://www.raventheatre.com/stage/astrangeloop/" target="_blank" ><b><u>A Strange Loop</u></b></a><b>” at Raven Theatre</b></h3><p>Raven’s recent production of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/07/14/octet-musical-lin-manuel-miranda-raven-goodman-dave-malloy-chicago-theater-summer" target="_blank" ><u>a cappella musical “Octet”</u></a> went so well that it transferred to the Goodman. Now Raven is mounting a full musical with the Chicago premiere of “A Strange Loop” by playwright and composer Michael R. Jackson. On paper, this show feels “Inception”-esque, a musical about a Broadway usher who’s writing a musical about a Broadway usher. It’s a brain teaser, but it won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 2020.</p><h3><b>Nov. 21: “</b><a class="Link" href="https://northlight.org/tribe-event-series/all-the-world/" target="_blank" ><b><u>All the World</u></b></a><b>” at Northlight Theatre</b></h3><p>This world premiere written by Lauren Gunderson, the most produced living playwright in America at the moment, will take us to another new theater. Northlight’s new home in Evanston has maintained an intimate feel in the theater itself, but the big beautiful lobby area is a reminder of the thought and intention that went into this state-of-the-art multimillion dollar facility. The production, directed by Chicago theater vet Jessica Thebus, is a backstage romcom about two actors trying to manage their relationship on and off stage during the holidays.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ac0000" name="image-ac0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ca57519/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F21%2Fb042f3f449cc8b583cafd156f6f0%2Ftheaterclubtargeted-260609-011.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d67226a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F21%2Fb042f3f449cc8b583cafd156f6f0%2Ftheaterclubtargeted-260609-011.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c69e18d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F74%2F21%2Fb042f3f449cc8b583cafd156f6f0%2Ftheaterclubtargeted-260609-011.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Theater reporter Mike Davis (left) moderates a WBEZ Theater Club panel discussion following a performance of playwright Hanna Kime’s “The Targeted” at Chopin Theater in Wicker Park on the North Side, Sunday, June 7, 2026. Answers to some frequently asked questions are below.</p><h4><b>What is Chicago Public Media’s Theater Club?</b></h4><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/04/08/wbezs-theater-club-returns-2026-lookingglass-steppenwolf-and-a-red-orchid" target="_blank" ><u>Theater Club</u></a> is a community of curious theatergoers who explore Chicago’s vibrant performing arts scene together with WBEZ theater reporter Mike Davis. The project piloted in Spring 2026 and we are excited to bring it back for Fall 2026.</p><h4><b>How does Theater Club work? </b></h4><p>Chicago Public Media, the parent organization of WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times, purchases tickets at a group discount for productions and sells them to participants, who attend a production in a group and are invited to discuss the work afterwards. Participants may buy tickets for a single show or multiple productions, depending on availability. WBEZ members are offered the first opportunity to buy the tickets.</p><h4><b>How much do tickets cost?</b></h4><p>Tickets are discounted, usually 50% off face value for each show. They include the show, the post-show talkback and a drink during cocktail hour. We don’t make a profit from Theater Club, and don’t expect to. But tickets are not free because we still believe it is important to support local theaters.</p><h4><b>How do you select the theaters?</b></h4><p>So far, the focus of Theater Club has been exploring new plays, so we have focused our attention there. A goal of Theater Club is to explore the city’s vast theater scene, including its storefronts, so we are not repeating any destinations from our Spring 2026 slate. We don’t accept solicitations from theaters. This is a menu of shows carefully curated by WBEZ’s arts desk.</p>

entries.title: QB Tyson Bagent doesn't travel with Bears, is 'week-to-week'
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/19/bears-training-camp-report-no-16-qb-tyson-bagent-remains-out" target="_blank" >Tyson Bagent</a> did not travel with the team to their joint practice in Cincinnati and is "week-to-week," coach Ben Johnson said. A source said earlier this week that the second-stringer hurt his hamstring during the Bears' preseason win against the Browns on Saturday. </p><p>Bagent's absence means the Bears have to make other plans for their next exhibition game — if not the next two. Johnson has said he'll evaluate whether to play his starters based on their performance at the joint practice. The Bears plan to play their starters heavily Thursday, though, which offers a clue that they won't play significant snaps Saturday. Another: Bengals coach Zac Taylor said Saturday he won't play his own starters.</p><p>Veteran Case Keenum, who had a perfect 158.3 passer rating against the Browns, would figure to get the majority of Saturday's snaps if the starters don't play. The only other quarterback on the team is rookie Miller Moss, who once played behind Williams at USC.</p><p>Johnson spoke about an hour before the start of the Bears' two-hour joint practice against the Bengals at the team's practice facility adjacent to Paycor Stadium. </p><p>Bagent didn't practice Sunday — nor did any other players who participated Saturday — and sat out practices on Tuesday and Wednesday.</p>

entries.title: Un hombre asesinó a una mujer a puñaladas y después se apuñaló a sí mismo en La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre está acusado de clavar un cuchillo de cocina en una mujer, matándola, antes de atacarse a sí mismo el martes en un apartamento de La Villita, según la policía.</p><p>No se han presentado cargos contra el hombre de 59 años, que resultó gravemente herido, según la policía. Fue arrestado y permanecía hospitalizado, según un informe policial.</p><p>Los agentes encontraron al hombre y a la mujer cuando respondieron a un reporte de una persona apuñalada a eso de las 11:35 p.m. en la cuadra 2500 al sur de Christiana Avenue, dijo la Policía de Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9a0000" name="module-9a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La mujer, cuya edad no se dio a conocer de inmediato, sufrió múltiples heridas por arma punzante y fue declarada sin vida en el lugar, dijo la policía.</p><p>El hombre, también apuñalado varias veces, fue trasladado al Hospital Mount Sinai, donde se encontraba en estado grave, dijeron las autoridades.</p><p>Por lo menos un cuchillo para cortar carne fue recuperado en la escena, según el informe, que también indicó que el hombre atacó a la mujer antes de apuñalarse a sí mismo.</p><p>Los detectives del Área 4 continúan investigando.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker declares 'BTS Day' in Illinois in honor of K-pop group’s visit to Chicago
entries.summary: <p>The arrival of BTS in Chicago will be marked with a new statewide commemoration, thanks to the K-pop group’s passionate fans.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has officially declared Aug. 27 and 28 “BTS Day” in Illinois, according to a proclamation he signed earlier this month. The superstar musicians will perform sold-out shows on those days at Soldier Field as part of the septet’s “Arirang” world tour. The governor was petitioned by the fan group Chicago BTS Army and the HANA Center, an immigrant advocacy nonprofit in Irving Park. Both groups also launched a campaign to turn the Downtown skyline “Borahae Purple” — in honor of a popular phrase (“I purple you”) associated with the group.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/01/13/bts-to-bring-world-tour-to-chicagos-soldier-field-aug-27-28" >BTS to bring world tour to Chicago’s Soldier Field Aug 27-28</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"Rather than simply celebrating a concert, the initiative highlights the profound, real-world civic impact of the band’s message of self-love, mental health awareness, and youth empowerment within Illinois," said Tameca Denson, lead organizer of the Illinois BTS Proclamation Initiative, in a statement.</p><p>The group is coordinating with building managers to finalize the details of the skyline illumination. The Willis Tower will be lit up in purple from 8:30-11 p.m. Aug. 27 and 28, Denson said.</p><p>“By coordinating this proclamation and proposing a purple skyline illumination, we are showcasing how a shared love of music can be reclaimed as a powerful pop-culture moment to elevate AANHPI visibility, support digital inclusion, and foster intergenerational connection across Chicago."</p><p>With thousands visiting Chicago for the concerts, the city is expecting an economic boost, along with opportunities for cultural exchange. Fan gatherings and cultural festivities are scheduled in Chinatown and throughout Downtown, including a two-day event at Buckingham Fountain from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. Aug. 27 and from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. entries.title: Bears training camp report No. 17: Bengals pressure gets to QB Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Thursday training camp practice with the Bengals:</p><p><b>Feisty tone</b><br>The teams practiced for more than two hours on a hot, muggy morning in Cincinnati, and it was bound to get contentious. There was an early scrap between Bears left tackle Darnell Wright and various Bengals defensive linemen, a widespread scrum among second-stringers on the Bears’ offense and Bengals’ defense in which coach Ben Johnson raced to the middle of the crowd to break it up and a third skirmish in which a Bears defender and Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow grabbed each other by the jersey.</p><p><b>Williams’ day</b><br>The Bears started with a botched snap between center Garrett Bradbury and quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> and ended with Williams throwing an interception in a two-minute drill. In between, Williams and the offensive line struggled with the Bengals’ pass rush quite a bit. After a rough start, the line played better and Williams began getting the ball out faster, but there still were some issues, especially managing three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence. Not only did Lawrence collapse the pocket, but he also stepped in front of a screen pass for an interception.</p><p>“They were running a lot of screens, so I felt this one,” he said. “I saw the running back in the corner of my eye and drifted over and did a little volleyball tip and came down with it.”</p><p><b>Tough to catch</b><br>The Bengals’ defensive line was strong throughout practice, but their linebackers and defensive backs had trouble staying on top of Bears running back D’Andre Swift and wide receiver Kalif Raymond. Raymond slipped into space for several catches in the middle of the field, and Swift weaved through the heart of the defense for a touchdown run in red zone work. Swift’s score elicited a loud f-bomb from a Bengals defender.</p><p><b>Special play</b><br>Johnson said he’d pay particularly close attention to special teams Thursday, and wide receiver Maurice Alexander gave him something to watch by returning a kickoff for a touchdown during a full-speed drill.</p><p><b>Nice grab</b><br>Bears rookie safety Dillon Thieneman was in the right place at the right time to intercept a pass from Burrow that went through tight end Mike Gesicki’s hands.</p><p><b>Secondary shuffle</b><br>Bears cornerback Tyrique Stevenson did limited work on the outside in his first practice in a week, and rookie Malik Muhammad worked at nickel. Cam Lewis was the first-string safety next to Thieneman.</p><p><b>Notable spectators</b><br>Many of the Bears’ injured players were on the sideline, including wide receiver Luther Burden, nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, defensive lineman Shemar Turner and new defensive end Marcus Davenport. Bears chairman George McCaskey and president Kevin Warren also were at practice.</p><p><b>What’s next?</b><br>The Bears have a preseason game Saturday against the Bengals, who won’t play their starters, and resume practice Tuesday at Halas Hall.</p>
