entries.title: Atlanta mayor accuses DNC of ‘abandoning Black voters’ as Atlanta and Chicago lose 2028 convention bids
entries.summary: <p>Chicago and Atlanta didn’t make the cut as finalists to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/01/23/chicago-pitch-2028-or-2032-democratic-national-convention" >host the 2028 Democratic National Convention</a> — and while Chicago’s host committee says it’s hopeful the city still has a chance at its 2032 bid, Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens is blasting out his criticism of DNC Chair Ken Martin's decision.</p><p>“They are afraid to leave their comfort zone and blind to the fact that the South is the answer,” Dickens said in a letter obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. “They are abandoning Atlanta, abandoning the South, and once again abandoning Black voters.”</p><p>Chicago’s host committee, which ran Chicago’s 2024 convention, said they were notified on Wednesday that the city didn’t make the final round. The DNC on Thursday released a statement from Martin that said Boston, Denver and Philadelphia are the three finalists for 2028. Martin said the three cities “presented incredibly strong bids” to host the convention and a decision would be made “in the coming months.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024-democratic-national-convention/2024/08/25/democratic-national-convention-chicago-brandon-johnson-jb-pritzker-cpd-larry-snelling" >The world turned its gaze to Chicago for the DNC. So how did the city fare?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Chicago put together a bid for both the 2028 and 2032 conventions, and the host committee hasn’t been given any information about that 2032 bid — although a source with knowledge of the planning said Chicago is still in consideration. They provided no details on the timing of that announcement.</p><p>Chicago’s host committee put up a strong front Thursday in reaction to the news, saying the city is still the strongest contender to host the 2032 DNC, citing its infrastructure and strength of the business, philanthropic and labor communities.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker would be at the end of his third term for governor come 2032, should he win in November, or he could choose another path and run for president in 2028. Either way, a source close to the governor said he will be involved in the 2032 bid process.</p><p>The Atlanta mayor’s office said they weren’t told about the decision before reading about it in the press Thursday. In a sharply worded letter, Dickens said the decision reflects that the DNC “does not consider Atlanta or Georgia relevant to the past, present, or future.”</p><p>“It seems that Ken Martin doesn’t even believe himself when he said that the road to the White House runs through the South,” Dickens said.</p><p>Dickens noted Atlanta hasn’t hosted a convention in nearly 40 years.</p><p>“At a time when Trump and the Supreme Court are minimizing Black electoral power we need a party that would come to Atlanta and galvanize the Southeast for 2028 and beyond,” Dickens said. “Real leaders produce for the present and the future.”</p><p>Of Martin’s leadership, Dickens said, he’s “ready for Democratic leadership that understands what every Democratic voter already knows: that this is a moment that demands we run toward battles and into the fight.”</p><p>The DNC declined to comment on Dickens’ letter. But the DNC voted last week to approve a slate of six early states to lead the 2028 presidential nominating calendar, including South Carolina with the first-in-the-nation primary on Jan. 22, 2028. </p><p>Pritzker and his top aides, along with Sen. Tammy Duckworth, Mayor Brandon Johnson and former Mayor Lori Lightfoot, helped secure the 2024 bid. A 2028 Chicago convention would have helped Pritzker’s nomination prospects in what is expected to be a crowded field of primary presidential challengers, if he chooses to run. </p><p>Those who were part of the Chicago bid said they showed that the Democratic city already has a “turnkey operation here.”</p><p>The 2024 DNC in Chicago generated $371 million in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024-democratic-national-convention/2024/10/17/democratic-national-convention-chicago-economic-impact" target="_blank" >economic impact</a> — and the host committee raised $97 million in cash or in-kind contributions and spent $83 million. Pritzker gave $2.6 million and first lady MK Pritzker donated $3 million. Of the $83 million reported in expenditures by the host committee, Development Now for Chicago, a total of $49 million was paid to Chicago-based businesses. Another $7 million went to firms based elsewhere in Illinois. The 2024 convention carried no debt to the city, the state or the DNC, and that’s considered a big selling point for Democratic leaders involved in the process.</p><p>Pritzker was largely credited with helping to land the 2024 convention and seemed to enjoy a huge spotlight brought on the city as its social chair of sorts. The governor said in May he would once again contribute if Chicago secured the convention, but would not say how much.</p>

entries.title: Man beaten, slashed in Greater Grand Crossing homicide
entries.summary: <p>Detectives are searching for an assailant responsible for a beating and slashing attack that killed a 59-year-old man Thursday morning in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood. </p><p>The man was found unresponsive in the 300 block of West 76th Street around 5:10 a.m. with cuts and trauma to his face, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was pronounced dead at the University of Chicago Medical Center, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: ComEd conspiracy case could go to trial all over again in February
entries.summary: <p>Two former ComEd officials<b> </b>could face trial all over again this February,<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/3/15/23641765/comed-bribery-trial-begins-federal-prosecutors-telling-jurors-hear-over-100-recordings" target="_blank" >four years after</a> the feds first told a jury<b> </b>they’d plotted to<b> </b>illegally influence<b> </b>former Illinois House Speaker Michael J. Madigan.</p><p>The case against former ComEd CEO Anne Pramaggiore<b> </b>and longtime Madigan ally Michael McClain returned to the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Manish Shah<b> </b>on Thursday, for the first time since<b> </b>an appeals court<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" target="_blank" >ordered the pair released</a> from prison<b> </b>and wiped out their 2023<b> </b>convictions.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Diane<b> </b>MacArthur told the judge it still isn’t clear how the case will ultimately be resolved. But she said, “we are ready to proceed to trial.”<b> </b>And Shah told the lawyers, “I want you to be thinking about February 2027."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/06/15/comed-boutros-mcclain-pramaggiore-broadview-six" >Chicago’s top federal prosecutor ‘weighing’ options after appeals court formally undoes ComEd convictions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“It’s obviously a case of some vintage,” Shah said. “Has been tried before. So in theory, people could get prepared and be ready for it.”</p><p>There are new faces this time around, though.</p><p>Pramaggiore<b> </b>shook up her defense team<b> </b>this week, enlisting onetime<b> </b>Chicago mob prosecutor<b> </b>T. Markus Funk and others<b> </b>to represent her. Funk told the judge his team has a mountain of evidence to review.</p><p>An early 2027 trial could<b> </b>be<b> </b>“difficult,” Funk said.<b> </b>But the judge pressed him and the other lawyers to consider it. Shah did not set a formal trial date.</p><p>The lawyers are due back in his courtroom in late October.</p><p>Funk once participated in Chicago’s historic Family Secrets<b> </b>mob prosecution, winning a<b> </b>top<b> </b>trial honor with his colleagues<b> </b>in 2008<b> </b>from then-Attorney General Michael<b> </b>Mukasey. He<b> </b>later<b> </b>shared book<b> </b>and article credits<b> </b>with U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros, before Boutros took office.</p><p>Now he might help take on the feds in one of the most significant Chicago corruption cases in recent memory — one already dealt a significant blow with the reversal this summer of Pramaggiore’s and McClain’s convictions.</p><p>The feds also have dropped a set of bribery charges<b> </b>from the case.</p><p>Defense attorneys Patrick Cotter<b> </b>and<b> </b>John Mitchell,<b> </b>who have long represented McClain, also made appearances during Thursday’s status hearing. Cotter told the judge he has retired and his appearance amounted to a “cameo." Mitchell will lead McClain’s defense, he said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/2/23697452/jurors-reach-verdict-in-comed-bribery-trial" >Jury convicts all four defendants in ComEd bribery trial — and fires a warning shot at Michael Madigan</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Meanwhile, MacArthur was joined in court by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Julia Schwartz and Richard Rothblatt. Two prosecutors who helped handle the original trial, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/03/04/lead-madigan-prosecutor-leaving-u-s-attorney-office" target="_blank" >Amarjeet Bhachu</a><b> </b>and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/11/10/superstar-prosecutor-convicted-madigan-burke-leaving-u-s-attorneys-office#:~:text=Assistant%20U.S.%20Attorney%20Sarah%20Streicker,the%20end%20of%20next%20month.&text=The%20Sun%2DTimes%20is%20a%20nonprofit%20newsroom." target="_blank" >Sarah Streicker</a>, left the U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>last year.</p><p>The ComEd conspiracy case dates back to 2020 and ended the record-breaking tenure of Madigan, the nation’s longest-serving state House leader.</p><p>Prosecutors say Pramaggiore and McClain — along with former ComEd lobbyist John Hooker<b> </b>and onetime City Club President Jay Doherty — conspired to illegally influence Madigan<b> </b>in a bid to benefit ComEd in Springfield.</p><p>Hooker and Doherty were convicted along with Pramaggiore and McClain, but did not pursue an appeal.</p><p>The utility wound up paying five Madigan allies<b> </b>$1.3 million<b> </b>over eight years through intermediaries,<b> </b>even though they did hardly any work for the utility, prosecutors have alleged.<b> </b></p><p>The conspiracy also involved<b> </b>the retention of<b> </b>the Madigan-aligned Reyes Kurson<b> </b>law firm and an appointment to the ComEd board of directors<b> </b>for businessman<b> </b>Juan Ochoa, according to the feds.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Eight weeks after the allegations appeared in a<b> </b>2020<b> </b>grand jury indictment, Madigan was forced to give up the speaker’s gavel in Springfield and soon left office. A grand jury <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/3/2/22958533/michael-madigan-indicted-charges-illinois-house" target="_blank" >indicted him</a> separately in 2022, and he is now serving a<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/06/13/mike-madigan-sentencing-hearing" target="_blank" >7 ½-year prison sentence</a>, in part for his role in the scheme.</p><p>The 2023 ComEd conspiracy trial featured about 50 witnesses<b> </b>over six weeks. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/2/23697452/jurors-reach-verdict-in-comed-bribery-trial" target="_blank" >Jurors<b> </b>eventually<b> </b>found</a><b> </b>Pramaggiore<b> </b>and<b> </b>McClain<b> </b>guilty<b> </b>of<b> </b>one count of conspiracy, as well as four bribery counts and four counts of falsifying ComEd’s books and records.</p><p>But the Supreme Court<b> </b>then<b> </b>used an Indiana corruption case in 2024<b> </b>to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/06/26/supreme-court-snyder-ruling-madigan-corruption" target="_blank" >limit the feds’ use of a bribery law</a> central to the indictments of Pramaggiore, McClain and Madigan. Because Pramaggiore and McClain went to trial before the high court’s ruling, they wound up on a different legal path than the former speaker.</p><p>Madigan went to trial three months after the high court's ruling. His own appeal has been unsuccessful, so far.</p><p>But judges from the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals<b> </b>struggled<b> </b>this spring<b> </b>to assure themselves<b> </b>that the convictions of Pramaggiore and McClain<b> </b>remained valid after the 2024 Supreme Court ruling. The trial record wasn’t clear.</p><p>So they ordered the pair released from prison<b> </b>in April<b> </b>and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/06/15/comed-boutros-mcclain-pramaggiore-broadview-six" target="_blank" >allowed prosecutors to try again</a>.</p><p>“Do not misread our opinion,”<b> </b>the judges wrote<b> </b>in June. “We are not suggesting that Pramaggiore and McClain are innocent, only that their convictions were flawed and that they have a right to see their sentences vacated.”</p>

entries.title: Hombre de los suburbios es detenido y dejado en custodia de ICE con cargos federales por portar bombas molotov
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre de los suburbios arrestado después de que una búsqueda policial encontrara bombas molotov en su mochila fue liberado con monitoreo electrónico, pero dos días después fue detenido por agentes del Servicio Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>Hamed Alsaidi, de 31 años, fue arrestado el 1 de agosto después de que oficiales de la Policía de Mokena lo registraran y encontraran ocho botellas de vidrio llenas con un líquido inflamable, con trapos metidos en las aberturas de las botellas, según el jefe de policía, Brian Benton, de Mokena.</p><p>Dentro de la mochila había un mapa de Orland Park con la palabra "mezquita" escrita en él.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-190000" name="module-190000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los agentes inicialmente encontraron a Alsaidi merodeando en una gasolinera en 187th Street y Wolf Road, dijo Benton. Los oficiales lo llevaron hasta una tienda cercana. Unas horas después, los agentes volvieron a ver a Alsaidi caminando en medio de 191st Street, cerca de LaGrange Road. Alsaidi dio a los agentes un nombre falso y fue detenido y registrado. Fue acusado de uso ilegal de un arma y de obstrucción a un agente policial.</p><p>Alsaidi, residente de Oak Forest, compareció en una audiencia de detención el 2 de agosto, cuando el juez Theodore Jarz, del Condado de Will, le concedió la libertad bajo fianza con monitoreo electrónico en virtud de la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/01/09/pritzker-illinois-house-speaker-welch-open-tweaking-safe-t-act-electronic-monitoring-rich-miller" target="_blank" >ley SAFE-T</a>, tras determinar que las condiciones podían mitigar los riesgos de su liberación.</p><p>Fue puesto bajo custodia de ICE dos días después, según el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS). Los funcionarios dijeron que Alsaidi, un inmigrante de Jordania, entró ilegalmente a Estados Unidos por California en marzo de 2024.</p><p>Los funcionarios federales dijeron que ICE presentó una orden de detención ante el Condado de Will el mismo día en que la Policía de Mokena arrestó a Alsaidi. Pero, en lugar de respetar la orden, las autoridades del condado lo liberaron el 2 de agosto sin notificar a ICE.</p><p>El lunes, Alsaidi fue acusado en la corte federal de posesión ilícita de un arma como delito grave y de obstrucción de identificación, según fiscales federales.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: Do legal challenges to hate speech protect Jews or threaten them?
entries.summary: <p>Bess Myerson, the first and only Jewish Miss America, was crowned on Sept. 8, 1945. In the hazy nostalgia that passes for historical understanding nowadays, people might assume her victory was due to the warm embrace that America gave all things Jewish after the horrors of World War II.</p><p>It wasn't.</p><p>James Loeffler starts his new book, "<a class="Link" href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250806079/exceptionalhatred/" target="_blank" >Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight Over Free Speech in Modern America</a>," with Myerson's win, noting that old habits die hard. Sponsors who traditionally embraced Miss America got cold feet. The Catalina Swimwear Company, which provided bathing suits for the contestants, withdrew its promised contract and scholarship.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>"Several corporate sponsors refused to hire a Jewish spokesmodel," he writes. "The Ford Motor Company reneged on its pledge of a gift of a new automobile."</p><p>Odd — you'd think that Henry Ford, who'd accepted a decoration from the Nazis, might be eager to put some distance between his company and his former pals. But no.</p><p>Such expectations wilt as you read Loeffler's book, which uses antisemitism to skillfully explore the difficulty of legally squelching haters in a nation whose First Amendment sanctifies free speech.</p><p>A significant chunk of Americans sympathized with Hitler before, during and after World War II — 70 new American antisemitic organizations appeared within a year after Myerson's win.</p><p>The first two sections of the book focus on events in Chicago. We think of the city as a liberal bastion. Now, maybe. But not in 1946.</p><p>"Chicago," the American Mercury wrote, "the birthplace of the German American Bund and scene of the greatest wartime seditious activities" — a Lane Tech grad was landed by U-boat during the war with a raft of Nazi spies — was on its way to becoming "the hate center of the nation and the staff headquarters for incipient American fascism."</p><p>Thus in February 1946, notorious antisemite Father Arthur Terminiello, on a coast-to-coast speaking tour promoting Christian Nationalism, held a packed rally on the West Side. Protesters rioted outside and Terminiello was convicted under a Chicago ordinance against disturbing the peace.</p><p>"The violence during that final hour would form the centerpiece of the legal trial to come," Loeffler writes. "Who were the victims and who were the perpetrators? Did the words inside the building stir the mayhem outside?"</p><p>Lower courts said yes and fined Terminiello $100. The Supreme Court overturned the conviction, with Justice Robert Jackson warning, in his famous dissent, that the Bill of Rights should not be allowed to become "a suicide pact."</p><p>The year of the ruling, 1949, saw another riot, one Loeffler calls "a postwar pogrom." Aaron Bindman, a union organizer, made the mistake of inviting Black associates to a party at his apartment in then working class, white Irish Englewood. The neighbors went berserk.</p><p>"Bloodied victims crawled along the streets pursued by mobs; journalists and civil rights officials from the ADL and a liberal Catholic group were assaulted. On the main Englewood commercial strip, mobs ransacked Jewish-owned stores, beating the store owners who tried to prevent them. Hundreds of policemen stood by idly. Most of those arrested were victims."</p><p>That's why I'm not as worked up as some over our current situation; I know my history.</p><p>The second section dissects the 1977 attempt by Nazis to march in Skokie. Here the book bogs down a bit, navigating every PR feint and legal twist, often conducted by Jewish ACLU lawyers defending Nazis. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Exceptional Hatred” by Johns Hopkins University Professor James Loeffler is being published next week by Metropolitan Books. It explores the difficulty of using law to constrain hate speech in a nation where free speech is sacrosanct. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Macmillan Publishers</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The last section begins in Charlottesville, Virginia, with the torchlit 2017 "Unite the Right" rally, leading to today, when Jews are being cynically played by the Trump administration as a pretext to shred civil rights.</p><p>"This hyperbolic assault on the teaching of American history turned anti-discrimination law into a cudgel to suppress critical discussion of racism's historical legacies," Loeffler writes. "Trump's second term delivered the cruelest irony: abusing Jewish fear to dismantle higher education. Without due process or court findings, the administration froze university funding, withdrew support for scientific research, and detained and deported foreign students for statements about Israel. Constitutional protections collapsed. What claimed to be the largest legal reckoning with antisemitism in American history doubled as its supreme trivialization — transforming a real problem into a political cudgel against universities, Palestinians, Muslims and immigrants."</p><p>What's next? The mainstream media flickers and fades, while "the internet persists as a rage factory where racists self-radicalize in digital echo changers."</p><p>Fair warning — "Exceptional Hatred" is a methodical, detailed legal history, recounting the serpentine court cases that stem from four jarring antisemitic incidents, three in and around Chicago. What hope Loeffler offers is that the law remains, battered and marginalized, but still a weakening guardrail against the president's bottomless hate-mongering and institution-wrecking. But the bottom line is clear:</p><p>"Antisemitic speech poses less danger than authoritarianism itself."</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams ends choppy day with interception as Bengals' pass rush hounds him
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> walked off the Bengals’ practice field Thursday afternoon steaming over a mistake on his final pass of the day. It had been a choppy performance to begin with, and this was an ugly way to end it.</p><p>Backed up to his own end zone in a two-minute drill after backup left tackle Theo Benedet allowed back-to-back sacks, Williams was under pressure in the pocket yet again. He saw tight end Colston Loveland open over the middle, but threw high and late — a recipe for disaster in that part of the field — and the ball deflected off Loveland’s hands to Bengals cornerback Jalen Davis for an interception.</p><p>It was the type of focus-related error that coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> has working with Williams to eliminate. His fundamentals must be correct even under duress, and that ball got away from him when he released it too high.</p><p>“I’ve got to bring the ball down,” Williams said, drenched in sweat after the Bengals chased him around for 2½ hours. “I got some pressure on the back side and just tried to check it down, get the drive going ... ended up missing.”</p><p>That’s the biggest thing still holding him back amid the strides he has made under Johnson, and a miss like that would be a nightmare in a game.</p><p>Williams was last in the NFL with a 58.1 completion percentage and second-worst in on-target passes at 69.8%, per Pro Football Reference, last season and that simply doesn’t work for Johnson. Not only does he want Williams to complete 70% of his passes in practices and games, he wants passes that lead his receivers into the open space that he created with his play designs.</p><p>That’s an absolute requirement if the Bears are going to chase Johnson’s goal of setting the NFL scoring record held by the 2013 Broncos at 37.9 points per game.</p><p>Williams did his best work in red-zone scenarios Thursday, at one point throwing touchdown passes on three consecutive plays, but plenty else needed improvement. The Bears will play the Bengals in a preseason game Saturday, and Johnson said he’d assess late Thursday whether he needed to get his starters some snaps.</p><p>The joint practice was far from reassuring.</p><p>The Bengals’ defense surely was amped up to face Williams after an offseason full of hype, including the prestigious Madden cover, and they were loud from the start. He’d better get used to that.</p><p>They flushed Williams out of the pocket on a play early in practice, sending him sprinting to the right sideline and throwing the ball out of bounds as defensive lineman T.J. Slaton taunted, “Where the (expletive) you going?” Later, after Williams hit rookie Zavion Thomas on the right sideline, defensive tackle Jonathan Allen shouted, “That’s a sack,” after his unit crashed the backfield but wasn’t allowed to hit Williams.</p><p>Three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence was Williams’ biggest problem throughout the day. The Bears eventually adjusted somewhat with the offensive line holding up better and Williams getting the ball out quicker, but Lawrence’s disruption was a constant concern.</p><p>Beyond the pressure he put on Williams, he also made a perfect read on a screen pass, stepped into the lane, “did a little volleyball tip,” he called it, and intercepted the pass.</p><p>The practice was a continuation of Williams’ turbulent trajectory. His passing was sharp the first week of training camp, then Johnson said he plateaued, but it started to pick back up over the past week.</p><p>“It's trending upward, and that's really what we want to see,” Johnson said before practice. “He's taken a lot of pride in where he's putting the ball throughout practice. You see it early on in our warm-up periods to routes on air, and it's translating over to the team periods as well, yet he still hasn't lost that stinger of being aggressive and trying to push the limits.”</p><p>Johnson saying that Williams’ accuracy is “trending upward” is one of the more complimentary appraisals he’s given in their two years together. He’s had no hesitation calling him out before.</p><p>More than anything, it comes down to Williams’ discipline. His talent is off the charts, but he has to harness it.</p><p>The essential points Johnson has been hammering are proper fundamentals, mainly that his feet are pointed at his target, and better anticipation of defenders. It’s on Williams to implement that, especially when the pocket starts breaking down. He called it a “mental and physical” battle.</p><p>When Williams was asked to grade his training camp so far, he described it correctly as a mixed bag. That’s undoubtedly a reflection of Johnson’s feedback.</p><p>“I’ve done a good job taking the coaching,” he said, pointing to that as the most important thing he can do right now.</p><p>But soon enough, all the learning and development must produce results. The Bears have a little over three weeks until their season opener and they want to be a Super Bowl contender. Williams can’t get them there if he’s still alternating steps forward and backward.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Lobbyist John Kelly, a mayoral candidate, vows to use relationships he's built to save a 'city in decline'
entries.summary: <p>Portraying Chicago as a crime-ridden “city in decline” and Mayor Brandon Johnson as the teachers union’s “tool,” mayoral <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/29/lobbyist-john-kelly-possible-chicago-mayor-bid-brandon-johnson-ballys-white-sox-katten-muchin-election" >challenger John Kelly </a>vowed Thursday to use the insider relationships he has built as a career lobbyist to deliver the resources the city needs.</p><p>If elected, Kelly promised to work toward adding 20 more ambulances, replacing “beat up” fire engines and trucks and hiring 1,000 more police officers to bolster a Chicago Police Department that Johnson has used his first three budgets to shrink by attrition.</p><p>Kelly is not saying precisely how he would pay for all of that when Chicago is facing a $90 million mid-year shortfall, a $1 billion gap in next year’s budget and a $36 billion pension crisis that has police and fire pension funds dangerously close to bankruptcy.</p><p>He would only talk in the broadest of strokes about reducing police overtime, cutting the mayor’s 154-member bodyguard detail and approaching private businesses, maybe even some of his own lobbying clients, for help.</p><p>“You need to find a way to spend money on equipment rather than all of the personnel that the mayor has paid for. If you have some of these unfunded positions that the mayor has in his office, you can cut 20 of those and buy five ambulances,” said Kelly, whose videotaped visits to Chicago firehouses for campaign videos has prompted an investigation by the Chicago Board of Ethics. The city’s ethics ordinance bars candidates for city office from intentionally using city property for political purposes.</p><p>“How about we talk to business people in Chicago and ask them, `Would you like to sponsor any ambulance? Can businesses in Chicago pony up and maybe buy an ambulance?’ Those are the kinds of things we need to discuss.”</p><p>Kelly, 53, is a consummate political insider.</p><p>For nearly three decades, he has lobbied on behalf of clout-heavy clients that do business with City Hall — the same people and companies he would have to deal with and say no to if he’s elected mayor. </p><p>“The number one guiding principle I will have is, `Is this a good deal for the taxpayers?’ because they’re gonna be my client the day I get elected,” Kelly told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“If [White Sox Chair] Jerry Reinsdorf walks in my office ... or Soo Kim, the owner of Bally’s, and asks me to do something … that’s not in the best interest of Chicago, I’m happy to tell them `no’ and I will tell them ‘no.’ … I can be conflict-free because I have an inner-core guiding principle: Is this right for the city of Chicago.’“</p><p>Kelly’s client list includes Bally’s, the debt-laden gambling giant that has stopped construction on all non-gambling elements of the $1.7 billion casino and entertainment complex in River West amid a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/08/17/ballys-chicago-casino-video-gambling-going-concern" >heated dispute</a> over a City Council majority’s decision to legalize video gambling terminals.</p><p>“They won’t be lining my pockets [as mayor] because I’ll have divested myself from my firm upon winning,” Kelly said. "As mayor, I need to look at, is the money we’re gonna make from the VGTs — the net terminal income that’s gonna go to the city — worth what Bally’s is gonna make?”</p><p>Noting that the tax on slot machine revenue is now nearly four times higher than it is on video gambling terminals, Kelly said he’s prepared to use his Springfield connections to lobby for a bigger cut for Chicago akin to the one-third share the state receives.</p><p>“A mayor … has to go to Springfield to do that, and this group’s incapable of doing it,” Kelly said of Johnson and his lobbying team.</p><p>Kelly describes himself as a moderate Democrat. But his wife, Julie Kelly, is an outspoken conservative who is a fixture on social media and right-wing podcasts.</p><p>She has made clear her support for President Donald Trump, the Jan. 6 protesters he pardoned, and the deportation campaign known as “Operation Midway Blitz” that swept through Chicago area neighborhoods.</p><p>“Opposites attract. … My wife and I disagree on a lot of things — not just about politics,” Kelly said. “This keeps being brought up by my opponents and I’m kind of thrilled that they’re doing that. It shows me and the taxpayers... that I’m a threat to them.”</p><p>The Kellys are currently named as co-defendants in a Will County lawsuit filed by a contractor who claims the company is owed nearly $650,000 on construction of their $4.4 million compound in Homer Glen.</p><p>“If we want to get out of the city for a weekend, it’s someplace we can go to. I can’t afford a mansion on Lake Geneva like a lot of my political opponents," Kelly said. "I don't know of anyone that's ever built a home that has not had a problem with their contractor."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-590000" name="html-embed-module-590000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_9016800b-c463-44e9-8dd3-1415f73b5501&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml" style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: What if the Sky had just been more like the Mystics?
entries.summary: <p>If you’ve watched any videos of the Mystics locker room this season, you know the vibe.</p><p>A bunch of 23-year-olds being lightly supervised by former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> forward Michaela Onyenwere, playing dodgeball with their coach and re-enacting scenes from “Love Island.”</p><p>They're the youngest team in the league, enjoying the process of building for the future, without much pressure to succeed right now.</p><p>The irony, of course, is that they’re succeeding anyway.</p><p>At 21-14, they have the best of both worlds: a great young core, draft capital galore and a chance to make some noise in the playoffs.</p><p>The frustrating part is, the Mystics haven’t done anything the Sky couldn’t have done themselves.</p><p>They drafted the obvious lottery choices in 2025 and 2026: Sonia Citron, Kiki Iriafen and Lauren Betts. They hired low-profile coaches with ties to Chicago. Head coach Sydney Johnson was one of Teresa Weatherspoon’s top assistants, while offensive coordinator Emre Vatansever was let go after stepping in for James Wade in 2023.</p><p>The Mystics did do one pretty special thing, though. One thing the Sky, and many other organizations, have a hard time doing: They accepted that rebuilding would take time.</p><p>Washington didn’t fight losing seasons in 2024 and 2025. They didn’t try to skip steps or accelerate their path to the playoffs.</p><p>They held onto their draft capital and put themselves in position to benefit from a losing record. Now Citron and Iriafen are All-Stars and the team is sitting solidly in the No. 6 seed, headed for the playoffs ahead of schedule.</p><p>The Sky did the opposite.</p><p>General manager Jeff Pagliocca has managed with a sense of urgency to compete immediately, uninterested in treating losing seasons as a necessary part of a long rebuild. So he traded away the Sky’s first-round picks in 2026, 2027 and 2028 to jump-start the process.</p><p>To his credit, he put together a roster that looked good on paper this season.</p><p>But holding on to your draft picks is kind of like disaster insurance. Pagliocca decided to go uncovered.</p><p>So when disaster struck — Rickea Jackson tore her ACL, the Sky kept blowing close games and point guard Skylar Diggins barely played — somebody else was positioned to benefit.</p><p>That somebody is Washington. The Mystics are set to receive the Sky’s 2027 lottery pick in exchange for their own and also own Chicago’s 2028 first-rounder.</p><p>The situation is especially painful because it’s not like the Sky have turned their back on young talent.</p><p>Kamilla Cardoso, their No. 3 pick in 2024, has developed into a solid pillar. Sydney Taylor, an undrafted guard plucked from the Polish league, was a home run. Aicha Coulibaly has also turned into a nice second-round find.</p><p>That success in identifying youngsters makes you wonder what this might look like if they had just leaned all the way into it.</p><p>Imagine if, rather than trying to speed up the process, the Sky had been content to wait. What if they had held onto their disaster insurance? What if they had surrendered to the tide of young talent coming into the league?</p><p>Pagliocca <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/03/amid-losing-season-sky-gm-jeff-pagliocca-still-sees-playoff-potential-and-an-underrated-young-core" >would argue</a> that if he hadn’t been so aggressive, he wouldn’t have landed Jackson. And it’s true: The deal that eventually gave Washington so much of the Sky’s draft capital brought Ariel Atkins to Chicago, who was later flipped for Jackson.</p><p>Maybe Jackson will be enough to vindicate the strategy in the end.</p><p>But for now, the Mystics are the ones having all the fun.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Previewing Week 1's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/03/high-school-football-schedule-ihsa-chicago-week-1-2026" target="_blank" >Week 1</a>. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3>No. 11 Maine South at No. 8 Batavia, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>It's another banner year for quarterbacks locally, and this will be a showcase for two of the best. Maine South senior Jameson Purcell is committed to Indiana after completing 70% of his passes last season for 2,572 yards and 30 touchdowns with seven interceptions. Batavia senior Michael Vander Luitgaren, a Wyoming recruit, threw for 2,708 yards and 31 TDs with four interceptions on 65% accuracy. The Bulldogs have an extra sense of urgency with coach Dennis Piron saying he's "99% sure" this is his last season.</p><h3>No. 2 Brother Rice at No. 18 Lincoln-Way East, 6:30 p.m. Friday</h3><h3></h3><p>It starts up front for Brother Rice with four-star senior Notre Dame commit Brayden Parks and five-star junior Kameron McGee anchoring the defensive line and senior Ethan Posey, a Miami (Ohio) commit, leading the offensive line. Some talented skill players also return in senior running back Jameson Davis (Army) and 6-5 junior tight end Jack McNamara. Lincoln-Way East had significant graduation losses, including state career passing yardage leader Jonas Williams. One notable veteran is Illinois-bound offensive lineman Mason Halliman.</p><h3>No. 22 Carmel at No. 10 Hersey, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Nebraska commit Trae Taylor, the consensus No. 1 quarterback nationally in the 2027 cycle, and receiver Greg Bess-Henning have transferred out of Carmel but the cupboard's not bare. Junior linebacker Jameer Miles and junior offensive lineman Wyatt VanBoehning are both four-star prospects. Hersey's Jake Nawrot, the No. 5 senior quarterback in the nation and a Kentucky commit, is back after throwing for 3,078 yards and 41 touchdowns with only two interceptions last season. His top target is junior Josh Riggs, who caught 11 of those TDs.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/19/michael-obrien-preseason-super-25-high-school-football-rankings" >Michael O’Brien’s preseason Super 25 high school football rankings</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/03/high-school-football-schedule-ihsa-chicago-week-1-2026" >High school football schedule for Week 1</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3>No. 16 Barrington at No. 25 Lyons, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>This is an interesting matchup of Class 8A powers aiming to compete for titles in two of the state's deepest conferences: the Mid-Suburban West (Barrington) and the West Suburban Silver (Lyons). Junior running back Lamar Osterhues is back after finishing with 1,319 all-purpose yards last season for the Broncos. The Lions also have a proven back in EJ Kuhlman, who ran for a program-record 246 yards against York last season. Tight end Owen Matela is a Miami (Ohio) commit.</p><h3>No. 1 Mount Carmel vs. East St. Louis, 7 p.m. Saturday at Hancock Stadium, Normal</h3><p>This will be the seventh game between the state's two winningest programs (East St. Louis has 864 victories, 32 more than Mount Carmel). The Caravan are 5-1 in the series and won 36-33 in 2023, the most recent meeting. Mount Carmel has more Power Four talent than any team in the state, including two Michigan commits (receiver Quentin Burrell and defensive back Tavares Harrington) and a Notre Dame recruit (linebacker Roman Igwebuike). East St. Louis' stars include running back Myson Johnson-Cook (Auburn), cornerback Raheem Floyd (Florida) and receiver Ronnie Gomiller (Cincinnati).</p>

entries.title: How much of a cancer drug do patients need? UChicago doctor, others challenge the FDA, drugmakers on dosing
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern University economist Chuck Manski studies decision-making amid uncertainty. That prepared him better than many other cancer patients to decide whether to stay on an immunotherapy treatment that was making him very ill.</p><p>For six months in 2022, Manski received monthly infusions of nivolumab to fight advanced melanoma. The drug ruined his thyroid gland, he said, requiring him to go on a special medication for the rest of his life, and caused severe dryness in his eyes, lips and mouth.</p><p>The federal Food and Drug Administration’s protocol for the drug called for an entire year of treatment, but Manski said his oncologist couldn’t explain why. It’s FDA-approved, “so that’s what we use,” he said he was told.</p><p>By that point, Manski showed no cancer signs or symptoms. After reading a lot of medical journal articles, he concluded that the intense side effects probably meant the treatment had done about all it could do.</p><p>“She couldn’t tell me a year was the optimal dose," Manski said of his doctor. "Nobody could. So I made my own diagnosis. I took myself off.”</p><p>Manski’s decision was in line with what doctors in Canada, Israel, Sweden and other countries already were doing: giving lower doses of nivolumab, which is sold under the brand name Opdivo, and of a similar drug, pembrolizumab — sold as Keytruda —, or giving them for shorter periods or over longer intervals than the FDA recommends. In India, oncologists found that as little as one-twelfth of the labeled dosage of nivolumab had a powerful impact on several cancers.</p><p>“There is incredible uncertainty in drug dosing,” Manski said.</p><p>His experience impelled him to join an informal yet determined community of researchers, doctors and patients pushing for extra studies to help patients and doctors find the right dosage for an array of cancer drugs. They point to evidence suggesting that taking smaller doses of some cancer drugs or remaining on them for shorter periods could save billions of dollars and prevent some of the worst side effects.</p><p>In a recent KFF survey, 43% of U.S. adults said they had skipped their medication in the past year because of cost. A 2022 Vanderbilt University study of Medicare enrollees found that 30% of cancer drug prescriptions went unfilled.</p><p>But dose-optimization studies rarely occur after the early stages of a drug’s development or once it’s on the market. By then, few parties in the U.S. healthcare system — beyond patients — have a stake in learning that a lower dosage could work as well while causing less harm.</p><p>Pharmaceutical companies have shown little interest in dialing back recommended dosages. Once they set a price for a drug, more sales mean more profit. One study that examined 29 expensive cancer drugs estimated that if minimum necessary dosages had been used in 2024, the U.S. healthcare system could have saved roughly $31 billion.</p><p>“Decisions aren’t always made with the best needs of the patients in mind,” said Dr. Matthew Goetz, a breast cancer researcher at the Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center in Rochester, Minnesota. "The bottom line is another reason."</p><p>Last year, Merck sold nearly $32 billion worth of pembrolizumab, a drug that’s FDA-approved for more than 40 cancer conditions. It accounted for almost half of Merck’s drug sales.</p><p>Bristol Myers Squibb brought in $10 billion from nivolumab, which works similarly to pembrolizumab in tweaking the immune system. Three important but often toxic breast cancer drugs — Ibrance, Verzenio and Kisqali — boosted revenue for Pfizer, Eli Lilly and Novartis by $4.1 billion, $5.7 billion and $4.8 billion, respectively.</p><p>Pembrolizumab usually is prescribed at a fixed dosage. Nivolumab is sometimes prescribed at a fixed dosage, sometimes based on the patient’s weight. If a patient is dosed less than what’s on the label, drugmakers generally get less money.</p><p>And they aren’t the only ones who lose out.</p><p>Through a federal program known as 340B, created in 1992 to subsidize the treatment of low-income patients, hospitals that treat a certain percentage of low-income patients can buy drugs at a steep discount while charging insurers or patients more. For Medicare patients, doctors are paid an additional 6% of the drug’s average price for each infusion.</p><p>From 2010 to 2024, cancer drug revenue to doctors and hospitals increased from about $9 billion to nearly $36 billion, according to research by Aaron Mitchell of the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. About half of those profits came from immunotherapy drugs like pembrolizumab and nivolumab.</p><p>“Pembrolizumab is the lifeblood of American hospitals,” said Dr. Mark Ratain, a University of Chicago Medicine professor and cancer doctor who is also chief hospital pharmacologist. “That’s why you don’t see hospitals in this country running to do trials that test lower doses.”</p><div News</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Merck spokesperson Julie Cunningham said the drug’s dosage recommendations were based on extensive testing.</p><p>“In a life-threatening and challenging disease such as cancer, it is critical that the dosing for a cancer therapy is established through well-designed clinical trials,” Cunningham said. “Changes in dose or duration that have not been similarly studied may potentially compromise the therapeutic effect.”</p><p>Still, some oncologists start patients off slowly on any of a variety of cancer drugs, though there might be concerns about lawsuits by a patient or their survivors over a prescription of lower-than-labeled dosages.</p><p>Dr. Kathy Miller, a professor of oncology at the Indiana University School of Medicine, said she routinely starts metastatic breast cancer patients with 400 milligrams of Kisqali daily for three weeks, with one week off, rather than the 600 milligrams recommended on the label. Sometimes, patients ask for the standard dosage.</p><p>“I have to tell them, ‘I don’t want to kill you,’ ” she said.</p><p>Insurers routinely challenge her lower-dosage prescriptions, Miller said, presumably because price rebates from the drug company are set to the standard dosage. To avoid endless phone battles with insurers, she prescribes 600 milligrams but tells patients to take only two of the 200-mg pills and save the third for the next cycle.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Researchers at Silicon Valley-based Revolution Medicines developed the promising new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, which doctors have hailed as a “revolutionary” new cancer treatment.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Revolution Medicines</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Focusing on ‘the shiny new drug’</h3><p>On May 31, at the annual meeting of the American Society of Clinical Oncology at McCormick Place, most of the audience of 8,000 rose in a prolonged standing ovation for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/26/pancreatic-cancer-daraxonrasib-early-access-treatment" >experimental drug daraxonrasib</a>. Patients with pancreatic cancer who took the drug, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/01/pancreatic-cancer-fda-daraxonrasib-experimental-drug-ben-sasse" >study presented that day,</a> lived nearly twice as long — a median of 13 months — as those receiving chemotherapy.</p><p>The next day, in a slightly smaller hall, Dr. Amol Patel, a medical oncologist from New Delhi, discussed studies in various cancers in which 20- or 40-mg doses of nivolumab biweekly — one-sixth or one-12th the recommended dosage — gave Indian patients several months to a year longer survival than patients who underwent chemotherapy, and with fewer side effects.</p><p>Fewer than 100 people attended Patel’s talk.</p><p>The ingenious development of daraxonrasib was big news since, until now, a pancreatic cancer diagnosis has been a death sentence. But, from a global perspective, the news out of India might be just as important.</p><p>At the ASCO meeting, “The focus is always on the shiny new drug,” said Dr. Daniel Goldstein, an oncologist and drug policy researcher at the Rabin Medical Center in Israel who has fought for a decade, with some success, to lower pembrolizumab dosages in hospitals.</p><p>The data from India offered a glimpse of what could be. But the studies Patel referred to compared ultralow-dosage immunotherapy to older chemo drugs. None compared ultralow doses against standard nivolumab or pembrolizumab treatments. In India, this would be a sterile exercise because full-dose treatments are beyond the reach of any but the very wealthy, said Dr. Vanita Noronha, an oncologist at Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai.</p><p>Bristol Myers Squibb has a program to make its drugs available in lower-income countries. But the company hasn’t been involved in the lower-dose nivolumab trials. It says the evidence suggests that nivolumab at a lower dosage or for a shorter duration harmed patients.</p><p>The Indian data is, to most, a mere curiosity. “Can we really give 20 milligrams as opposed to 240?” asked Dr. Jessica Bauman of the Fox Chase Cancer Center in Philadelphia. “The only way we know for sure is a randomized study between the low dose and the highest.”</p><p>And such trials are unlikely to occur. That means only poorer countries are going to host “this groundbreaking research,” Ratain said. “The Indians may have better immunotherapy than we do.”</p><p>Clinicians in Europe, where maximizing healthcare dollars has long been a priority, have taken a middle course, studying lower but not ultralow doses of immunotherapy.</p><p>Dr. Michel van den Heuvel, a pulmonologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, is leading a study comparing the standard nivolumab dosage for lung cancer patients with one that is as much as 50% lower. He considered giving the low doses half as frequently, but that would have raised ethical concerns and led to a more cumbersome research protocol, van den Heuvel said.</p><p>In the United States, researchers led by a group at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston are taking another tack, evaluating whether patients who’ve done well on 27 weeks of pembrolizumab can stop taking it rather than doing the additional six months per FDA protocol.</p><p>In the federal Veterans Health Administration, which has more leeway in testing money-saving medical procedures, doctors saved $1.5 million, about 10% of the previous pembrolizumab cost, over two years at three Veterans Affairs hospitals where they implemented a pilot program to dose patients less frequently, said Dr. Garth Strohbehn, a University of Michigan and VA oncologist.</p><p>It saves money and requires fewer visits for veterans who often live hours from the hospital, according to Strohbehn, who said, “It also helps other patients because it opens more slots for infusion.”</p><p>Julie Gralow, ASCO’s executive vice president and chief medical officer, has made testing dosage a priority. She’s working with scientists in India on an ambitious clinical trial to compare standard nivolumab with four lower dosage levels.</p><p>Gralow also is leading an $11 million trial, supported by the federally funded Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, to see whether breast cancer patients can be effectively started on lower doses of the drugs Kisqali and Ibrance, which, along with Verzenio, are in a class of key breast cancer drugs known as CDK4/6 inhibitors.</p><p>“We want to maintain efficacy, but we also want patients to have excellent quality of life,” she said. Especially for patients with advanced cancers, where absolute cure is unlikely, “It’s our job to make sure we’re not compromising quality of life with higher doses that are unnecessary.”</p><p>In 2021, at Ratain’s urging, Dr. Richard Pazdur, who led the FDA’s cancer drug division for many years, launched Project Optimus, intended to get companies to conduct dosing studies that are more precise before launching the large clinical trials they use to obtain FDA approval for new drugs.</p><p>The agency issued nonbinding guidelines for dosing studies in 2024 and has incorporated Project Optimus principles into the approval process for new cancer drugs, according to Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the federal Department of Health and Human Services. For example, two dosing regimens were evaluated for each of four lung cancer drugs — fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan, tarlatamab, zongertinib and sunvozertinib — and the lower dose with fewer toxicities was approved in each case, she said.</p><p>The FDA usually can’t compel a drugmaker to conduct dose-ranging studies after a drug’s approval, Hilliard said, and, by law, the agency does not influence drug pricing.</p><p>Future drugs should have better dosage information, Bauman said, but “newer drugs will probably be just as expensive at lower doses.”</p><h3>Financial toxicity</h3><p>Verzenio’s side effects made Allegra Warfield feel so sick, tired and bewildered, she said, that she considered suicide. She switched to Kisqali, which was tolerable, until last September, when coverage of the drug stopped despite her monthly premium payment of $6,000. The cash price for Kisqali was at least $16,000 a month.</p><p>After fighting her insurer for three months, Warfield, 42, sold her house and belongings in Palm Desert, California, and moved with her fiancé to Durham, North Carolina, where they’d found what they considered a reasonable insurance plan.</p><p>The cancer, the side effects and the unpayable bills were bad enough. The lack of good answers for her treatment made everything worse, she said.</p><p>“I was left to research these medications on Facebook and Reddit," Warfield said. "The only people talking about the daily reality of these drugs were other patients. But I wanted the studies. I wanted practical guidance.”</p><p>Stories like these launched a new life mission for Dr. Kelly Shanahan, who was an OB-GYN in South Lake Tahoe, California, until side effects from a breast cancer drug caused her to lose sensation in her hands. Unable to practice medicine, Shanahan became a patient advocate who works with a group called the Patient-Centered Dosing Initiative. In 2021, Shanahan developed profound fatigue (“worse than caring for a newborn baby while being on call in my solo practice”) within a few weeks of going on Ibrance. Lowering the dosage caused her worst symptoms to lift.</p><p>After gathering countless anecdotes, her group has approached drug companies seeking data — so far with little success — that might indicate what percentage of patients have needed dosage reductions and how they fare on lower doses.</p><p>“If going down two dose levels cuts effectiveness by 50%, patients need to know that while making decisions. If it doesn’t, they need to know that,” Shanahan said — even if it means “the companies won’t make as much money.”</p><p>Shanahan said the data could be found in clinical trials and post-market studies.</p><p>But if drug companies won’t provide the necessary studies, the University of Chicago's Manski said, governments should.</p><p>“The knowledge to be gained is a common good,” he said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://kffhealthnews.org/about-us" target="_blank" ><i><u>KFF Health News</u></i></a><i> is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism on health issues.</i></p>

entries.title: Bengals WR Ja'Marr Chase touts 'aggressive' Jaylon Johnson after joint practice
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Bengals receiver Ja’Marr Chase was still fuming after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/20/bears-training-camp-report-no-17-bengals-pressure-gets-to-qb-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >Thursday’s practice</a> that a ball didn’t come his way when he sprung open during team drills against the Bears.</p><p>Perhaps he was annoyed by the cornerback across from him, too.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ Jaylon Johnson played Chase close, who is just two years removed from leading the league in catches, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns, during the joint practice.</p><p>“Real good corner,” Chase said. “Pretty aggressive on a couple plays.”</p><p>Too aggressive?</p><p>“I get jumped every day,” Chase said. “I get jumped for a living. I’ve got many yards getting jumped at the line. That’s not aggressive.”</p><p>Chase’s best catch — a jump ball up the right sideline — came with Tyrique Stevenson in coverage.</p><p>“On the back end, you want to see stickiness in coverage,” coach Ben Johnson said before practice. “We want to be able to stay attached and try to make plays on the football. Our calling card a year ago was the takeaways. It would be great to get a couple takeaways."</p><p>Johnson’s performance was a good sign after he missed most of last year with a series of groin injuries.</p><p>“I've seen improvement out of Jaylon,” defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said Wednesday. “I've seen some flashes that say, ‘Man, he's looking a little bit more like what you expected him to look.’”</p><h3>T.J. ramping up</h3><p>Linebacker T.J. Edwards hurt his calf while training off-site before training camp. He’s still not participating in full practices.</p><p>He said Thursday he didn’t know exactly when he’ll be full-go, saying he trusted the trainers and coaches to ramp him up correctly. He’s still scarred by last season, which he started with a hamstring pull that cost him all but 10 games. He then broke his leg in the playoff game against the Packers.</p><p>“I'm not used to missing anything,” he said. “So I'm not letting that happen here.”</p><h3>Highway signs</h3><p>The Bengals’ outdoor facility is located a block from Paycor Stadium — players have to walk in cleats from their gameday locker room to the three fields — and is located underneath a series of overpasses. Fans watched practice from the overpass — technically, the end of the Clay Wade Bailey Bridge, which connects Ohio to Kentucky — on Thursday. One even managed to wriggle to the opposite side of the fencing that lined the street.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>• After Johnson said he’d pay particularly close attention to special teams, receiver Maurice Alexander returned a kickoff for a touchdown in a full-speed drill with the Bengals covering.</p><p>• Running back Kyle Monangai, who hurt his knee Sunday and is considered week-to-week, stayed back at Halas Hall for rehab work.</p><p>• Safety Elijah Hicks, who's on the physically-unable-to-perform list, was padded up as part of his return-to-play protocol.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore entries.title: Four firefighters injured, 3 seriously, in Back of the Yards blaze
entries.summary: <p>A Back of the Yards neighborhood fire that erupted Thursday morning in a vacant home left four firefighters injured — three of them seriously. </p><p>The residential building started burning about 11:30 a.m. on the second floor of a wooden two-flat in the 5400 block of South Justine Street, according to a Chicago Fire Department spokesperson. </p><p>While fighting the fire, four firefighters were injured, three seriously, according to the spokesperson. The fourth was listed in good condition at a hospital. </p><p>The building was not demolished and though the fire did not spread to other buildings, it extended into the attic. </p><p></p><p>The cause of the fire remains under investigation. </p>

entries.title: ¡Empate total! La serie estelar entre los Cubs y los White Sox termina 3-3
entries.summary: <p>Empate.</p><p>A los aficionados del béisbol de Chicago puede que no les guste, pero no lo olvidarán.</p><p>Con los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> venciendo a los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> 3-0 el miércoles en Wrigley Field, la mejor serie Crosstown de todas terminó en un empate 3-3. Sí, leíste bien, la mejor, desde que el juego entre ligas empezó en las Grandes Ligas en 1997.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f90000" name="module-f90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>(No, no me tocó ver a los “Hitless Wonders” de 1906 sorprender a los Cubs en seis juegos en la Serie Mundial. Seguro que fue todo un espectáculo).</p><p>“Es algo así como un empate, supongo, en cierto sentido”, dijo el novato jardinero izquierdo Sam Antonacci, con sus habilidades matemáticas a pleno. “Solo seis juegos en total, equipos realmente buenos enfrentándose. Siento que necesitamos más juegos para decidir el ganador.”</p><p>Esa es la actitud.</p><p>Antes de la temporada, la rivalidad conocida como el Crosstown clásico ya contaba con una buena lista de momentos estelares. El primer jonrón de desempate, conectado por Brant Brown de los Cubs en 1998. El grand slam de desempate —el primero de ese tipo en el juego entre ligas en las Mayores —pegado por Carlos Lee de los White Sox en 2001.</p><p>Los White Sox remontando desde un 8-0 en contra, impulsadas por un par de cuadrangulares de Paul Konerko, para ganar en 2002. El batazo largo de Aramis Ramírez de los Cubs para un walk-off en 2008, cuando ambos equipos rumbo a los playoffs estaban en primer lugar. El estallido de Eloy Jiménez de los White Sox en el noveno contra sus ex empleadores en 2019. Y claro, los jonrones de desempate de Christopher Morel en 2023 y de Mike Tauchman en 2024.</p><p>Pero la serie de esta temporada en ambos lados de la ciudad rindió a un nivel tan alto que pareció prender fuego a toda la fanaticada del béisbol en Chicago. Eso no pasa muy seguido, en gran parte porque los Cubs y los White Sox coinciden en ser competitivos aproximadamente con la misma frecuencia con la que se ve un eclipse solar total.</p><p>Pero con los White Sox en primer lugar de la División Central de la Liga Americana (sí, están en una división terrible) y los Cubs encaminándose hacia el primer comodín en la Liga Nacional (no, no van a alcanzar a los Brewers), el foco estuvo intenso, y se desató un caos embriagador.</p><p>¿Cómo superar la manera en que los White Sox lucharon en mayo después de perder el primero de tres juegos en Rate Field? En el Juego 2 de esa serie, Munetaka Murakami se presentó con estruendo frente a los aficionados de los Cubs que habían estado ignorando sus hazañas, despachando un par de jonrones.</p><p>Tres jugadores más de los White Sox —incluido el llamativamente emergente Miguel Vargas— dieron una paliza. Luego, en el cierre, los equipos se cambiaron cuadrangulares de tres carreras en la novena para forzar entradas extra, y el escenario quedó servido para que el improbable héroe Edgar Quero la sentenciara para los White Sox con un jonrón de dos carreras en la décima.</p><p>Pero la superestrella de los Cubs, Pete Crow-Armstrong —tres meses después de abrir la boca en la valla del jardín de Rate y meterse en problemas— subió todo un nivel con su actuación en Wrigley, donde abrió los Juegos 1 y 2 con jonrones y terminó el primer juego en la décima con un bambinazo de dos carreras.</p><p>Su compañero Alex Bregman añadió un imparable de desempate en la novena la noche siguiente en un juego que terminó alrededor de la medianoche tras una suspensión por lluvia en las entradas finales. Mucho drama.</p><p>Para conseguir un empate en la serie —después de ir 2-12 ante los Cubs de 2023 a 2025— los White Sox necesitaron un héroe en el cierre. Entró José Urquidy, un nombre de una Serie Mundial pasada que más recientemente se había difuminado en el olvido.</p><p>En 2024, el diestro se sometió a la cirugía Tommy John. Hace menos de cuatro semanas, los White Sox hicieron un trato con los Pirates para conseguirlo, enviando a cambio a un relevista llamado Felix Doroteo. Como regla general, cuando te cambian por algo que suena más a un totopo que a un prospecto de alto nivel, las expectativas de ti tienden a ser bajas.</p><p>Pero Urquidy, días después de ser convocado desde Triple-A a los 31 años, entró en la tercera entrada y lanzó seis entradas sin permitir carreras, pareciendo durante un par de horas el mejor abridor de cualquiera de los dos rosters.</p><p>¿Quién podría haberlo previsto?.</p><p>“Sin duda, ha sido muy duro”, dijo, negando con la cabeza, después de que las cámaras de televisión se retiraron de su casillero en el vestuario visitante. “Me tomó dos años llegar a este punto, sentir que mi cuerpo está listo para estar en las Grandes Ligas”.</p><p>¿Y ahora?.</p><p>“Me siento saludable”, dijo. “Siento que puedo con todo. Estoy muy feliz de tener esta sensación”.</p><p>Fue una serie de temporada de otro tipo. Para muchos de los Medias Blancas, duros de espíritu pero inexpertos, fue una atmósfera sin precedentes.</p><p>“Arriba, sin duda”, dijo el jardinero central Tristan Peters. “Muy eléctrico. Hay gente peleando en las gradas. Hay abucheos. Hay gritos de alegría. Hombre, estuvo intenso”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: After spike in HIV cases in Chicago, new data shows a decrease in new infections
entries.summary: <p>HIV infections in Chicago have started to again decline following a spike in diagnoses in 2024, according to data released Thursday by the Chicago Department of Public Health.</p><p>The number of new HIV diagnoses — 504 — decreased by about 38% compared to last year, according to the city’s HIV midyear data brief. HIV infections had previously been on the rise in Chicago after a two-decade drop, with infections growing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/03/31/hiv-aids-infections-up-in-chicago-after-years-of-decline-as-cases-rise-among-latinos" target="_blank" >29% between 2022 and 2024</a>.</p><p>In 2024, nearly half of the new infections were among Latinos, which marked the first time the racial and ethnic group accounted for the most new diagnoses.</p><p>The new data shows that Black individuals accounted for most of the infections, about 47%, according to the city’s data from 2025. Latinos account for 34% of the new infections.</p><p>City officials cautioned that the new data was considered provisional and may shift once it’s finalized.</p><p>"It reflects the ongoing work CDPH does with our community and healthcare partners to get Chicagoans tested, connected to care, and engaged in HIV prevention,” said Dr. Garth Walker, the city’s public health commissioner, in a news release. “With health equity as our guiding star, the trends are promising. The exact numbers may shift between now and December, but this points in a positive direction for what we expect to confirm near the end of the year."</p><p>The number of AIDS diagnoses also decreased so far by nearly 23%, according to the city’s data.</p><p>Community groups, particularly those that lost funding this year for HIV prevention efforts, have been critical of how the city is dispersing funds to address HIV and AIDS. On Wednesday, a group of advocates protested outside of the Chicago Board of Health meeting in the Loop.</p><p>About three dozen people circled outside where the meeting was taking place chanting, “These budget cuts have got to go.”</p><p>Kendall Moore, from the AIDS Healthcare Foundation, said they were calling on the city’s public health department to restore funding, in particular for community groups that served the South and West sides. </p><p>“These are real people that we’re talking about,” Moore said. “These are real systems that have critically adjusted. There are folks who have fallen out of care. And the question remains: Does the city really care about these communities?”</p><p>Many advocates held signs asking the same question.</p><p>The AIDS Healthcare Foundation has a pending lawsuit in Circuit Court of Cook County against the city’s Department of Public Health over its handling of Ryan White HIV/AIDS program funds. The lawsuit alleges that the city improperly denied their funding proposal and did not follow regulations surrounding how the funds are dispersed.</p><p>In May, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/22/ige-resigns-commissioner-public-health-johnson-arwady" target="_blank" >Dr. Olusimbo Ige </a>resigned as commissioner of the city’s health department. Moore said they had not yet met with <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/08/mayor-brandon-johnson-taps-new-public-health-commissioner" target="_blank" >Walker who was tapped in July</a> to replace Ige.</p><p>Moore said advocates plan to continue protesting until funding is restored to community groups like the South Side Help Center.</p><p>“We’re going to continue to do everything that we possibly can to get the money restored, so that folks can receive a healthy bill of health and do what we can in our power,” Moore said.</p><p>The next court hearing is scheduled for Monday.</p>
