entries.title: With PPP fraud case looming, son of Chicago’s ex-top cop avoids suspension over chaotic arrest
entries.summary: <p>The son of former Chicago police Supt. Terry Hillard avoided discipline for his role in a chaotic arrest at a South Side police station after ex-top cop Larry Snelling pushed back on the findings of the city’s police oversight agency.</p><p>Officer Dana Hillard, however, remains stripped of his policing powers in another disciplinary case in which he’s accused of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/03/cops-accused-ppp-fraud-domestic-violence-sons-former-chicago-police-superintendents" target="_blank" >bilking the federal Paycheck Protection Program</a>, a pandemic-relief program that was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief/2026/07/15/ppp-fraud-pandemic-chicago-police-inspector-general" target="_blank" >overrun with fraud</a>, records show.</p><p>As the younger Hillard faces potential dismissal in that case, he caught a break last month in the other investigation centering around an on-duty imbroglio.</p><p>The Civilian Office of Police Accountability initially found that he’d broken department rules by failing to de-escalate the situation and engaging in an “unjustified” argument with someone who was arrested while trying to file a report over a crash.</p><p>“You came here for our f---ing help,” Hillard reportedly said. “You should’ve called your motherf---ing brother.”</p><p>The incident played out at the Wentworth District on Oct. 30, 2023, after a father and son caused an uproar when they were told they’d missed their turn to file the report and would have to wait longer, COPA said. </p><p>Hillard and a sergeant came to check on the commotion, and the sergeant began tussling with one of the men while Hillard brought the other outside, COPA said. When the second man returned, he smacked Hillard on the shoulder and was taken into custody during a struggle. Both men were charged with criminal trespass to state land.</p><p>Hillard was accused of getting into a “heated verbal exchange." Body camera footage showed another officer had to physically intervene to keep Hillard from getting any closer to the pair, according to COPA.</p><p>Allegations that Hillard wrongfully arrested the man or grabbed his neck without justification weren’t sustained, COPA said. But the oversight agency recommended that he face up to a 29-day suspension for hurling profanities and failing to bring the temperature down — allegations Hillard admitted to. </p><p>Still, Snelling rejected the findings in a letter to COPA Chief Administrator LaKenya White in January. The then-superintendent argued that Hillard’s actions amounted to a "reasonable response to an escalating and volatile situation.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ad0000" name="image-ad0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f84ba7b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/475f3d8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/460bfb5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Police Supt. Larry Snelling at the police headquarters, Tuesday, Oct. 17, 2023. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/460bfb5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8bb86eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/460bfb5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1600x898+0+84/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F9b%2Fe2a219fe4a07a3d5349b9e99c3a7%2Fsnelling.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Then-Chicago police Supt. Larry Snelling at police headquarters in October 2023.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“COPA noted that Officer Hillard used some profane language during the encounter; however, the use of profanity does not render the verbal altercation unjustified, particularly in the context of managing two aggressive and noncompliant individuals,” Snelling wrote.</p><p>COPA then amended its findings on July 15, wiping out the sustained allegations while recommending that Hillard undergo training in de-escalation.</p><p>Steffany Hreno, COPA’s deputy chief administrator, said in a brief document that the agency’s original recommendations were appropriate but were altered “in the interests of settlement.”</p><p>Meanwhile, City Hall’s inspector general has recommended that Hillard be fired for allegedly getting more than $18,000 in fraudulent PPP funds and filing bogus applications for other pandemic-relief loans.</p><p>Those allegations were detailed in a July 2025 report by then-Inspector General Deborah Witzburg, who noted that Hillard had also made “false statements” about those applications in an effort “to obstruct” her office’s investigation.</p><p>The inspector general’s office also urged the police department to have Hillard added to the city’s do-not-hire list, according to the report. By then, the department had “preliminarily agreed” with the recommendations and directed the law department to draw up formal charges seeking Hillard’s dismissal.</p><p>But, more than a year later, such charges haven’t been made public. Hillard continues earning $119,154 while working in the alternate response section, a unit that handles non-emergency calls and includes cops with disciplinary issues.</p><p>At least 36 Chicago police officers have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ppp-paycheck-protection-program-covid-relief/2026/08/04/ppp-fraud-crystal-cooper-cps-chicago-public-schools-paycheck-protection-program" target="_blank" >found to have defrauded the PPP program</a>, according to reports by inspector general’s office.</p><p>Hillard didn’t respond to a request for comment.</p><p>He joined the Chicago Police Department in 2006 after working as a campus cop at Northwestern University, state law enforcement records show. So far, he hasn't followed in his father’s distinguished footsteps. </p><p>Terry Hillard was appointed police superintendent in 1998 by Mayor Richard M. Daley, and he remained in the role until he retired in 2003. He also co-founded Hillard Heintze, a security risk management firm that worked with corporations, government agencies and “prominent individuals,” according to an online biography.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-340000" name="image-340000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54c9e28/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+125/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb9%2F72%2F6f75db7f41fba9695ad8cd2eac3b%2Fbailey-cst-0427-15.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd61307/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+125/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb9%2F72%2F6f75db7f41fba9695ad8cd2eac3b%2Fbailey-cst-0427-15.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6a524e7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+125/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb9%2F72%2F6f75db7f41fba9695ad8cd2eac3b%2Fbailey-cst-0427-15.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Interm Police Supt. entries.title: Cook County records 13th heat death of 2026, more than doubling previous decade high
entries.summary: <p>Cook County has recorded its 13th heat death of the year, now more than doubling the highest counts of the last decade, according to the Cook County Medical Examiner’s office.</p><p>The 69-year-old Chatham man died July 2 of cardiovascular disease, ethanol poisoning and heat exposure</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis</u></a> of medical examiner data previously found Cook County has had more deaths related to the heat in 2026 than any other year in the last decade, and the number continues to go up. Heat deaths previously peaked in Cook County in 2019 and 2022 when there were six deaths each.</p><p>Ten of the 13 have been Chicago residents, and all but one — which was in the East Side neighborhood — have been on the South and West sides.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-3e0000" name="html-embed-module-3e0000"></a><div style="min-height:866px" id="datawrapper-vis-Upn49"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Upn49/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Upn49"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Upn49/full.png" alt="Heat-related causes have killed thirteen so far this year in Cook County, with ten dead in Chicago (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The first heat-related death this year occurred July 1, and most others followed throughout the month as the area saw several waves of severe heat.</p><p>Earlier this month, Otto Kedzior, 64, died of cardiovascular disease <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/05/cook-county-10th-heat-related-death-2026" target="_blank" ><u>complications and heat stress</u></a> in the 1000 block of South Wood Street, authorities said.</p><p>Others whose deaths have at least in part been attributed to the heat this year include Otto Kedzior, 64; Claremont Little, 94; Joseph Huff, 65; Robert Feldon, 77; Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; Daniel Machnikowski, 69; Victor Ferguson, 48; and David P. Sopys, 46.</p><p>While the majority of the deaths have been older residents, younger people have been among the grim count.</p><p>Jesus Rodriguez <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/13/heat-death-july-heatwave" target="_blank" ><u>died July 17</u></a> due to hyperthermia and environmental heat exposure, in addition to cocaine toxicity, according to the medical examiner’s office. The 33-year-old is the youngest of the more than dozen deaths tied to the heat this year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-a00000" name="html-embed-module-a00000"></a><div style="min-height:529px" id="datawrapper-vis-BaAyK"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BaAyK/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BaAyK"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BaAyK/full.png" alt="Thirteen people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in at least a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 'Just turn the lights on:' Gary residents endure historic power outage that nears two-week mark
entries.summary: <p>As Lisa Bryant and her mom, Jackie, pulled up to The Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry, they thanked the pastor and volunteers loading their trunk with fresh groceries that would feed them for the next few days: bread, cheese, deli meats and canned goods.</p><p>The Bryants are among the thousands of residents in Gary who remain without power after severe storms tore through northwest Indiana last week, causing a historic outage that left much of the region in the dark.</p><p>“This will at least nourish us for a couple of days,” Bryant said as a box of food was loaded into her car.</p><p>Like many others, Bryant is unclear when power will be restored.</p><p>“It's completely dark,” said Bryant, 47. “It's been cool enough for us to raise the windows, but it's been terrible not knowing when our lights will turn on.”</p><p>Thursday marked 10 days since the majority of Gary residents have been without power after strong storms ripped through the city.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/outages/power-outages" target="_blank" >NIPSCO</a>, which serves all of Gary, said more than 22,000 of its 35,800 customers, or 61%, remained without power Thursday. The utility company said power would be fully restored in Gary by Tuesday, Aug. 25, but Bryant said the company has repeatedly pushed back the restoration date. However, local efforts, like the food distribution event at The Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry, 5829 W. 15th Ave., are helping residents like the Bryants get through the blackout, which has also taken a financial toll.</p><p>Bryant said the outage has spoiled all of her refrigerated and frozen food, and she can’t afford a generator to keep her appliances running.</p><p>“Even if I could afford the generator, the person on the next street got their generator stolen off the porch,” she said. “If I do spend the money for a generator and somebody steals it, I'm still back in the same darkness.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-810000" name="image-810000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lisa Bryant looks over at Jackie Parker Bryant during a grocery and food handout at Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry at 5829 W. 15th Ave. in Gary on Thursday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Pastor Valerie Clarke said the church distributes groceries at least once a month, but the need in the community has grown amid the ongoing power outages.</p><p>“The community is totally devastated,” Clarke said. “But while we don't have power, we're grateful that we still have our lives.”</p><p>Clarke said the church is doing what they can to help those in need.</p><p>“No one should have to go hungry,” she said.</p><p>Bryant said the outage has also cost her income. She works as a food service manager at a nearby school, but classes citywidehave been canceled until power is restored. </p><p>The Gary Community School Corporation did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>While Bryant has been without power, her parents have had to spend extra money to run a generator that keeps their medical equipment operating and their medications refrigerated.</p><p>Parker Bryant and her husband, Alan, both rely on CPAP machines to sleep, while Alan, who has diabetes, needs to keep his medication refrigerated.</p><p>“We’re retired, we don’t have money to spare,” said Parker Bryant, 75.</p><p>Businesses in Gary have also been hit hard by the outage.</p><p>Local restaurants, gas stations, grocery stores, banks, along with other private businesses are still currently without power. Many remained closed while others were operating in a limited capacity.</p><p>Saleh Mohamed, owner of the Clark gas station at 2295 Richard Gordon Hatcher Blvd., said he had to close the business for four days before he could get a generator.</p><p>He’s using two generators to power the business, but they’re only enough to keep the gas pumps, cash register and lights running.</p><p>“It’s unbelievable,” he said. “We thought it was going to be a day or two and we’d be good to go.”</p><p>Mohamed said that when the business reopened Sunday, they were overwhelmed by customers looking to fill up their cars or gas cans for generators. Business has since slowed, but he said the station is one of only a few in the area that remain open.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure a restoration timeline for businesses, as NIPSCO is prioritizing residential areas over businesses.</p><p>Hospitals have been restored, though, due to their critical need. Officials said they have been told that power for other businesses and residents could possibly be restored by Tuesday.</p><p>Mayor Eddie Melton acknowledged Wednesday how frustrating and difficult the outages have been for residents and said that a $100,000 donation from Hard Rock Casino Northern Indiana would support ongoing storm recovery efforts across the city.</p><p>“You have been patient, you have been been understanding and you’ve been frustrated with the delays, just like me and my family,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/19/gary-power-outage-deadly-storms" target="_blank" ><u>Melton said Wednesday</u></a>. “Progress is being made, power is actively being turned on. But many residents are still suffering without power.”</p><p>The funds will provide direct assistance to residents affected by the storm and help distribute critical supplies, including food, water, health and hygiene products, and cleaning and debris-removal materials.</p><p>Bryant said Gary residents were resilient, but after nine days without power, they had endured enough.</p><p>“Just turn the lights on,” Bryant pleaded. “That’s all I ask.”<br></p>

entries.title: Illinois Republicans set state fair sights on Gov. JB Pritzker and 'flat-out crazy' Democrats
entries.summary: <p>SPRINGFIELD — It was a different political boogeyman being put on blast Thursday at the Illinois State Fair, where Republicans sharpened their attacks against incumbent Gov. JB Pritzker in his bid for a third term with a rematch this November’s against GOP nominee Darren Bailey.</p><p>And as much as Pritzker and his fellow Democrats <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/19/chris-welch-state-fair-illinois-house-sexual-harassment-harry-benton" target="_blank" ><u>lampooned Donald Trump a day earlier during their own fairground rally</u></a>, Bailey and his Republican colleagues mostly steered clear of mentioning the president — who remains unpopular in most of the state — while zeroing in on cost-of-living, public safety and education issues.</p><p>“That is what Illinoisans are concerned about,” Bailey said. “They're not concerned about the lies that JB’s smearing. They've woken up over the last four years. They realize the damage that JB Pritzker is doing to the state. They realize it because they're living it and they're feeling it.”</p><p>Heeding his running mate’s call to put “petty differences aside” in a party grasping for relevance, Cook County GOP chair and lieutenant governor candidate Aaron Del Mar said he buried his own hatchet with the southern Illinois farmer Bailey. Now the Chicago-area/downstate ticket is posing a simple question to voters who haven’t sent a Republican into statewide office since 2014.</p><p>“Are you better off now than you were seven-and-a-half years ago? You absolutely are not, and we are sick and tired of it,” Del Mar said in a fiery fairground speech. “We are tired of being pushed around. We are tired of being attacked. We are tired of being taxed, and we're not taking it anymore.”</p><p>Bailey lost to Pritzker in a landslide four years ago, but he assured “our friends in the Chicagoland area, it is completely different — completely different — than it was four years ago.</p><p>“They're getting it because they can't afford to live there, they don't feel safe and they know their schools are failing,” Bailey said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" id="gallery-720000" launched a TV ad campaign blasting Bailey’s “extreme MAGA views,” the longtime Trump supporter downplayed his ties to the president who has dragged down the GOP ticket in suburban areas of DuPage County that previously served as the base of the Illinois Republican Party.</p><p>“The president of the United States has nothing to do with the problems that Illinois is having right now,” Bailey told reporters. “We need new leadership, and the people need to realize that JB Pritzker has and is and will continue to fail them if we let him have another term.”</p><p>Pritzker’s campaign trolled Republicans’ day at the fair with several staffers donning dinosaur costumes holding signs declaring “Dinosaurs against Darren Bailey,” poking at the curriculum at a Bailey-founded school teaching that humans coexisted with the prehistoric reptiles.</p><p>Bailey wouldn’t say whether he agrees with the United States Geological Survey and the body of science that holds that some 65 million years elapsed between the extinction of dinosaurs and the rise of man.</p><p>“Go ask Fred Flintstone,” Bailey said, referring to Pritzker. “Let him explain it, because he needs to be focused on spending money on getting the message out on how he is going to make Illinois more affordable, safer, and fix our schools. And he's refusing to do that.”</p><p>Nor was the specter of Trump raised by U.S. Senate candidate Don Tracy, who said his own party is “far from perfect — but the other side is flat-out crazy.” Instead, Tracy raised the specter of communism.</p><p>“My Chicago opponent in this election, Lt. Gov. [Juliana] Stratton, and her Democratic Socialist allies like [New York City] Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani, [Chicago] Mayor [Brandon] Johnson, Bernie Sanders, Stacy Davis Gates and the two Democratic Socialists who just won the Democratic primaries for U.S. Senate in Michigan and Florida,” Tracy said.</p><p>“We believe in legal immigration, they’re for open border. We believe in law and order. They're for social justice, whatever that means — which I think means defunding police and letting career criminals roam free.”</p><p>Illinois House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, was one of the few speakers of the day to pounce on questions around Democratic House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch’s handling of sexual harassment allegations against disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield.</p><p>“Speaker Welch knew about the allegations. He did nothing, and then spent $1.4 million to put that creep back in office. He got him reelected. And what did that do? It opened up the door for Harry Benton to harass more women,” McCombie said.</p><p>Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/20/bob-grogan-illinois-republican-party-new-chairperson-dupage-county-auditor" >GOP Chair Bob Grogan</a> suggested Welch could be “the next Mike Madigan,” but said his party has now more material to work with to gain ground in Illinois beyond bashing the federally convicted former speaker.</p><p>“We were a one-trick pony. We just ripped on Mike Madigan. Deserved, but that was our campaign strategy,” Grogan said. “The Democrats, they are a one-trick pony. All they do is rip on Donald Trump. He's not on the ballot, either.”</p>

entries.title: White Sox rookie Braden Montgomery is holding his own, but still working to unlock star potential
entries.summary: <p>For a 23-year-old who only spent one full season in the minors, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> rookie right fielder Braden Montgomery is holding his own.</p><p>He’s an above-average defender at a spot that’s been a revolving door for the franchise for over a decade, highlighted by his howitzer of a throwing arm which provided a key outfield assist in Wednesday’s Sox victory at Wrigley Field. Scouts worried about the swing-and-miss in Montgomery’s game as a prospect, but his strikeout rate (22.3%) is almost league average and his pitch selection is an early strength. Switch-hitters like Montgomery are always developing two different swings and his right-handed cut isn’t producing yet (.554 OPS), but it worked fine for a game-breaking two-run double in the Crosstown finale.</p><p>“He's figuring this out and we're just trying to win a baseball game, he's doing everything he can to contribute to do that,” said manager Will Venable. “But I think there's a version of him which is exciting, in which he's going to be pulling the ball hard in the air, and doing some damage.”</p><p>Venable used the word “cerebral” to describe the young outfielder in spring, and Montgomery agreed it fits. As such, he’s plenty aware of the duality of his current state. Montgomery is a productive starter on a playoff hopeful Sox team, and his .265/.349/.400 line swinging as a lefty has him batting middle of the order against opposing right-handed starters. Simultaneously, four home runs in 60 games does not reflect the power potential offered by his quick hands and NFL free safety-like build.</p><p>“I’m just trying to find the balance of doing everything now that I can and focusing on that,” Montgomery told the Sun-Times. “How to win the games in the moment, while also not being satisfied with where I’m currently at and using my training to take those steps forward and try to get to where I want to be.”</p><p>Montgomery discusses tweaks to his swing as mere pit stops on a never-ending road of self-improvement, rarely romanticizing any one adjustment. But he’s noticeably more upright in his stance these days, a move aimed at allowing Montgomery more space to explode forward in his stride.</p><p>Sox hitting coaches see Montgomery’s 59.9% ground ball rate, which would lead MLB if he had enough plate appearances to qualify, as a product of not catching pitches out in front. They view MLB's Statcast measuring his bat speed out as a below-average 69.6 mph as evidence that his readily apparent physical gifts have yet to be maximized.</p><p>They also see it as par for the course.</p><p>“It's not just [velocity], it’s [pitchers releasing the ball with] seven feet of extension [from the pitching rubber],” said Sox hitting director Ryan Fuller. “They just do not see that in the minor leagues. For Braden and all the guys, when you're able to hit the ball hard on a line in the air, you're catching it in a good contact point. His contact points when he's a little bit late, get a little bit too deep. Once he understands ‘This is when I need to start my swing, it was never that early in the minor leagues, but I'm going to have to make the adjustment to start even earlier,’ he's going to be able to get to those spots and hit really productive balls.”</p><p>In managing to provide roughly average offense and good right field defense as a rookie, Montgomery is a little like the 2026 White Sox; not bad at all, but more exciting for what it implies about better days ahead. Such is his potential, the Sox would probably keep playing him even if he were actively struggling. Such is Montgomery’s nature that few traces of satisfaction are evident.</p><p>“With a game like baseball, every day is a clean slate,” Montgomery said. “You just let things be as they are, and that's when subconscious changes happen and bad habits set in.”</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Even after shutout loss, hitting coach Derek Shomon has White Sox offense leading AL in runs per game
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> offense deservedly receives a lot of credit for the team’s surprising 2026 turnaround. Even playing .500 baseball since June 1, the Sox lead the American League in runs scored per game.</p><p>But with a lineup built around loose and long-levered athletes who slug fastballs, their production can be boom-or-bust in nature, as evidenced by <b>Grant Holmes</b> and three relievers holding the White Sox to one hit in Thursday afternoon’s 2-0 loss to the Braves.</p><p>First-year hitting coach and Glenview native <b>Derek Shomon</b> employs a style built around blunt feedback with an offense light on hitters older than 26, and heavy on high-maintenance and/or still developing swings.</p><p>“You want to establish those relationships, especially as a newly-hired hitting coach, as early in the offseason as possible, so you're not wasting time trying to figure out when you should say something,” Shomon said. “We are in the dog days. We are in a pennant race, and meaningful adjustments still need to be made, calibrations still need to be had. So you don't want to [bleeping] walk on eggshells and feel like the relationship is not there.”</p><p>After their first half exploits, getting Sox hitters back on track has some easier reference points, even if they’re delivered with tough love.</p><p>“Success leaves clues,” Shomon said. “When you've had success, you can refer back to those times and use that as a blueprint to get you back to feeling crispy and sexy.”</p><h3><b>Brazobán struggling upon arrival</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Recently acquired reliever <b>Huascar Brazobán</b> broke a streak of being scored upon in three-straight appearances on Thursday. But only because the runner he allowed to score went on starter <b>Anthony Kay</b>’s tab, and the 93.9 mph exit velocity on <b>Austin Riley</b>’s seventh inning RBI single was the softest of the three batted balls he allowed.</p><p>Three more years of team control was part of the appeal when Sox GM <b>Chris Getz</b> sent prospects <b>Gabe Davis</b> and <b>Zach Franklin</b> to the Mets for the 36-year-old Brazobán at the trade deadline, but immediate bullpen help was a bigger part.</p><p>Instead, the right-hander looks off his game.</p><p>“We’ve got to get him competitive in the zone,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>. “He's learning a new environment, whatever it might be, we’ve just got to get him comfortable and on track. So we'll continue to work through that. He's going to be in big spots here coming up, he's one of our guys back there.”</p><h3><b>Rotation updates</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Venable plans to have <b>Erick Fedde</b> and <b>Jose Urquidy</b> take their next turns in the rotation, be it a traditional start or behind an opener, with the former throwing a bullpen Thursday ahead of likely pitching on Sunday against the Mets. But with the Sox still in a stretch of 16 consecutive games without an off day, unexpected needs could arise.</p><p><b>Davis Martin</b> (right middle finger blister) should make a Triple-A rehab start soon, before being eligible to come off the injured list on Aug. 29</p><p><b>Drew Thorpe</b> hasn’t pitched in the majors in two years due to injury, but has a 2.70 ERA in 10 innings across two Triple-A rehab starts. Venable referred to Thorpe as “a depth option.”</p><p>In honor of his niece Annabella, who is battling brain cancer, Kay threw six innings of two-run ball Thursday while donning cleats decorated by patients at Lurie’s Children’s Hospital.</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Former CPS principal gets more than a year in prison for near decade-long invoice fraud scheme
entries.summary: <p>A former CPS principal has been sentenced to a little more than a year in federal prison on wire fraud charges for a nearly decade-long scheme to defraud multiple school networks and nonprofits out of more than $1 million.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Lindsay C. Jenkins sentenced Brian Metcalf, a former CPS network chief and previous principal of Gage Park High School and Field Elementary, to a year and one day in federal prison Wednesday, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Former CPS vendor Kimberly Maddox was sentenced to two years in prison last month and consultant James Campbell, who also participated in scheme after it had begun in Indiana, was also sentenced to a year and a day.</p><p>They’re all on the hook for $1,099,200 in restitution payments to the various institutions they defrauded. A CPS inspector general report earlier this year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/07/cps-watchdog-report-onlyfans-waste-fraud-investigation-education-false-grant" target="_blank" ><u>uncovered more on the trio’s fraud plots</u></a>.</p><p>“Administrators who use their position to enrich themselves and deprive CPS families of critical resources will not be tolerated, and neither will vendors who steal from CPS,” Inspector General Philip Wagenknecht said in a statement Thursday.</p><p>From 2012 to 2017, Metcalf worked with former CPS vendor Kimberly Maddox to generate false invoices for goods and services — such as grant-writing training and student financial aid counseling — that were never provided. They split the proceeds after receiving payment from the district, the office said.</p><p>Metcalf and Maddox later admitted to the scheme as part of a plea deal in a federal case against them involving a similar plot to defraud a charter school network across the Indiana border after he left CPS in 2018.</p><p>In 2025, Metcalf and Maddox admitted they used the same false invoice strategy at Tindley Accelerated Schools in Indiana, where Metcalf was chief executive officer from 2019 to 2022. The scheme netted them nearly $1 million before they confessed to doing the same at CPS, which garnered $88,500.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/07/cps-watchdog-report-onlyfans-waste-fraud-investigation-education-false-grant" >Former CPS principal and network chief defrauded district of nearly $89K, watchdog finds</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bengals QB Joe Burrow preaches urgency; Caleb Williams should listen
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow hadn’t scuffled in practice since college. But when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo grabbed his jersey after a pass that rookie safety Dillon Thieneman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/20/bears-training-camp-report-no-17-bengals-pressure-gets-to-qb-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >intercepted Thursday</a>, Burrow held Odeyingbo’s shirt and started barking.</p><p>The whole thing lasted two seconds — just enough time for Burrow’s teammates to run to his defense.</p><p>‘‘I don’t care what we do,’’ Bengals wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase said. ‘‘We just better [freaking] protect Joe.’’</p><p>Burrow could laugh about it later — ‘‘Fun to go at it a little bit,’’ he said — but there’s no questioning the urgency he is stressing during training camp.</p><p>‘‘I’m tired of saying, ‘Next year, next year, next year,’ ’’ he said. ‘‘This is it. Your life is too short to keep pushing things down the road. I’m trying to instill some urgency and some intensity in everybody to go and be great every day and try and go make it happen.’’</p><p>He wasn’t speaking to Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, but Williams would be wise to listen. The Ghost of Quarterbacks Past knows the value of winning while you can — and how fleeting true championship opportunities can be.</p><p>Burrow is no longer the cigar-smoking hotshot who won the Heisman Trophy at LSU before being drafted No. 1 overall. Amazingly, he’s turning 30 in December.</p><p>Time, then, is of the essence.</p><p>‘‘I’m trying to put it out in the world; I’m trying to manifest it,’’ he said. ‘‘I’m trying to show our guys the urgency that I have and that I want us to have as an organization to go and make it happen. You can keep pushing it down the road, or you can talk about it now and say, ‘This is the year.’ ’’</p><p>Burrow is anywhere between the second- and fifth-best quarterback in the league. His team has climbed the mountain, though, and slid back down it.</p><p>The Bengals went to the Super Bowl in Burrow’s second season, even leading the Rams in the final two minutes. They reached the AFC Championship Game in his third season and lost to the Chiefs by three. They haven’t been back to the playoffs since.</p><p>Beset by injuries in two of the last three seasons, Burrow has gone 19-16 as the starter since the end of the 2022 season. Without him, the Bengals have gone 5-11.</p><p>Williams has nowhere near that résumé through his first two seasons. If anything, his first season — the Matt Eberflus disaster — was one for the burn pile. But the Bears have now what the Bengals did when they went to the Super Bowl: standout pass-catchers playing on rookie contracts and an up-and-coming quarterback. Both teams have questions about their defense. Neither can compete for a title without its quarterback being a star.</p><p>Before practice, during which Burrow was particularly masterful in the red zone, Bears coach Ben Johnson praised Burrow’s pocket awareness, ability to recognize coverage and get the ball to his best receivers.</p><p>‘‘This guy is like a surgeon back there,’’ Johnson said.</p><p>Since he was in college, Burrow has kept an eye on Williams and took him to dinner while Williams was on a recruiting trip to LSU.</p><p>‘‘He made some incredible plays, and they always seemed to come up in huge spots,’’ Burrow said. ‘‘To have him make those plays in those big spots, it’s good for the league, it’s good for Chicago, it’s good for everybody.’’</p><p>Burrow knows what would be good for him, too.</p><p>‘‘We have to step up and make something happen this year,’’ he said. ‘‘We’re working very hard for it. The urgency’s very high in the locker room. You can feel it. It’s palpable.’’</p><p>It’s now or never.</p><p>‘‘That’s how I’m treating it,’’ Burrow said.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bc0001" name="list-bc0001"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, items=[{type=Image, publishDate=August 20, 2026 04:38 PM, _styledTemplate=null, imageAlignment=null, isFeatured=false, anchorId=promo-660000, timestamp=1787261905000, authors=[{authorPageUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/patrick-finley, ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/author/byline/AuthorByline.hbs, jobTitle=[{items=[Chicago Bears reporter]}], bio=[{items=[Patrick Finley covers the Bears and the NFL for the Sun-Times after previous stops in Arizona, Florida and California.]}], media=[{ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, alt=patrick-finley-0.jpg, narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/3e/6853c67f16af2c0c2ea207670528/patrick-finley-0.jpg, width=512, height=512}, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/3e/6853c67f16af2c0c2ea207670528/patrick-finley-0.jpg, width=512, height=512}}], name=[{items=[Patrick Finley]}]}], description=[{items=[Burrow is no longer the cigar-smoking hotshot who won the Heisman Trophy before being drafted No. 1 overall. entries.title: Complaint deemed unfounded against state lawmaker surfaces in downstate legislative race
entries.summary: <p>SPRINGFIELD — A former staffer for a Democratic downstate legislator went public Thursday with salacious allegations of harassment and misconduct against her former boss that were deemed unfounded last year by a top legislative watchdog.</p><p>Republicans say self-described progressive Laura Jackson “felt ignored by Springfield” after she filed formal complaints against state Rep. Amy “Murri” Briel, D-Ottawa, but Democrats dismissed the charges as “a misleading political attack” in a district that’s expected to be closely contested in the Nov. 3 election.</p><p>In a press release shared by a GOP-aligned consultancy firm and the campaign of Briel’s Republican challenger, Liz Bishop, Jackson accused Briel of unwanted “repeated sexual advances, workplace drug use, harassment and retaliation” while working in the legislator’s district and campaign offices.</p><p>The ex-staffer claims in a a 43-minute interview posted online that Briel told Jackson she “could be Briel’s sexual ‘prize’ after winning the election,” supplied Jackson with Adderall in a frantic run-up to the 2024 election, smoked marijuana while working in Springfield and gave weed to staff as a “bonus.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ad0000" name="image-ad0000"></a> <picture Amy “Murri” Briel, D-Ottawa.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Illinois General Assembly</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey said Jackson filed a complaint with his office in April 2025, and that he deemed it unfounded a month later. McCuskey declined to outline the allegations in the complaint, but said Jackson waived her right to confidentiality.</p><p>He sent the results of his investigation to the bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission, which would have to vote to release the report publicly. A commission spokesperson didn’t immediately return a message seeking comment.</p><p>Briel called for the immediate release of McCuskey’s report and rejected the allegations from what she termed a “malicious and false campaign video.”</p><p>“Liz Bishop can’t run on her blind loyalty to proven abuser Donald Trump, so her campaign is recycling malicious claims previously proven to be false,” Briel said in a release. “The statements in the video produced by her MAGA political operatives were previously taken to the Legislative Inspector General in 2025 and were found to be without merit.”</p><p>Asked to respond to McCuskey’s dismissal of Jackson’s complaint, Bishop said in an email that the “situation certainly underscores the need for ethics reform in Illinois and a more robust process for review of complaints and victim support.”</p><p>“Laura Jackson felt ignored by Springfield and sought assistance elsewhere. After working hard to promote a candidate she felt obligated to correct the record,” Bishop said.</p><p>Republicans claimed Jackson’s case as another test of House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/19/chris-welch-state-fair-illinois-house-sexual-harassment-harry-benton" target="_blank" ><u>has faced criticism</u></a> even from within his own caucus for how he handled sexual harassment allegations against ex-state Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield.</p><p>Benton resigned last month following accusations of making lewd comments to a lobbyist at a River North bar, but Welch was aware of a separate complaint against Benton about two years earlier when the speaker directed $1.4 million into his reelection campaign.</p><p>Unlike the initial complainant against Benton, Jackson chose to file a formal complaint with the inspector general.</p><p>TaQuoya McConnico, executive director of the House Democrats’ political arm, called it “a clever political tactic by House Republicans, who have made Rep. Briel one of their top targets.</p><p>“Like many political attacks designed to generate headlines, it leaves out a critical fact: these allegations were investigated by the Inspector General’s Office and found to be unfounded,” McConnico said in a statement. “We will not allow a misleading political attack to distort Rep. Briel’s record or diminish our commitment to the values she has consistently fought for.”</p>

entries.title: Agentes intimidaron y admiten que investigaron a un hombre sólo por enviar una crítica negativa a ICE
entries.summary: <p>En junio pasado, dos investigadores empleados por el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) se presentaron en la casa de David Streever en Rochester, Nueva York. Streever no estaba en casa, así que le dejaron una nota.</p><p>Esa <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.2.pdf" target="_blank" >nota</a>, presentada como una advertencia oficial del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE), está en el centro de una <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.0.pdf" target="_blank" >demanda por la Primera Enmienda</a> que Streever presentó el mes pasado, alegando que agentes de ICE lo investigaron y lo amenazaron por sus críticas, protegidas constitucionalmente, a su jefe.</p><p>Este mes, el gobierno <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/17/nx-s1-5934692/dhs-free-speech-investigations" target="_blank" >respondió</a> a la demanda de Streever, confirmando sus alegaciones mientras intentaba rebatirlas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0d0000" name="module-0d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El 26 de enero, dos días después de que agentes del DHS le dispararan mortalmente al manifestante de Minneapolis, Alex Pretti, Streever envió un <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.1_1.pdf" target="_blank" >correo electrónico</a> enojado a Todd Lyons, el entonces director interino de ICE. Streever llamó a Lyons "un ser humano monstruoso", lo comparó con el funcionario nazi genocida, Reinhard Heydrich, y predijo que lo atormentaría "la vergüenza por su propia patética debilidad" por defender el disparo a Pretti "hasta el último día de su vida".</p><p>La evaluación que hizo Streever de Lyons fue dura, por decir lo menos. Pero no dijo nada que pudiera interpretarse razonablemente como una amenaza de violencia.</p><p>Sin embargo, Brent Goodwin, subdirector de investigaciones en la Oficina de Responsabilidad Profesional de ICE, afirma que el correo de Streever "tenía matices potencialmente amenazantes" y que "podía representar un riesgo para la seguridad".</p><p>Porque "la Oficina de Responsabilidad Profesional de ICE no tenía ninguna información sobre el señor Streever cuando llegó el correo electrónico", destacó Goodwin en una <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.20.1.pdf" target="_blank" >declaración</a> del 5 de agosto, se "determinó que era necesario llevar a cabo una investigación de ICE".</p><p>Lo que ocurrió después tiene poco sentido si los investigadores de ICE —que ni siquiera intentaron contactar a Streever hasta cinco meses después de su correo— intentaban resolver un legítimo "problema de seguridad". Pero sus acciones son completamente comprensibles si lo que buscaban era intimidar a un crítico de ICE.</p><p>"PUEDE ESTAR INFRINGIENDO LA LEY FEDERAL", decía el "<a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.1.2.pdf" target="_blank" >AVISO DE ADVERTENCIA</a>" que dos agentes dejaron con la esposa de Streever en Rochester el 23 de junio. Citaba dos estatutos, uno relacionado con las <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/115" target="_blank" >amenazas de violencia</a> contra funcionarios federales, y el otro que convierte en delito <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/119" target="_blank" >revelar</a> "información personal restringida" sobre ellos con la intención de intimidar o incitar a la violencia.</p><p>Streever no había violado ninguna de esas leyes. Pero el aviso decía que ICE tenía "motivos para creer" que su correo a Lyons "podría constituir una violación del Título 18 del Código de los Estados Unidos", que <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/event/113th-congress/house-event/LC21283/text?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >incluye</a> más de 1,500 delitos.</p><p>El documento pidió a Streever que "retire y/o suspenda de inmediato el comportamiento mencionado anteriormente". Añadía que "la recepción de este Aviso se tendrá en cuenta, si usted continúa participando en cualquiera de las actividades delictivas descritas arriba".</p><p>Además de entregar el aviso, agentes de DHS intentaron, sin éxito, interceptar a Streever en el Aeropuerto Internacional John F. Kennedy cuando regresaba de un viaje a Finlandia con su hija de 7 años el 25 de junio. También intentaron contactarlo repetidamente en persona y por teléfono en el hotel de Nueva York donde se hospedó esa noche.</p><p>Después de eso, dice Goodwin, ICE se dio por vencido y cerró el caso el 30 de junio porque "todas las pistas investigativas" se habían "agotado". ICE hizo eso aun cuando sus agentes nunca lograron entrevistar a Streever para determinar "si él representaba una amenaza", que, según Goodwin, era el objetivo de la investigación.</p><p>Al solicitar la desestimación de la demanda de Streever, los abogados del gobierno <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184/gov.uscourts.dcd.294184.20.0.pdf" target="_blank" >reconocen</a> que su correo a Lyons "expresó con palabras sus desacuerdos con un funcionario de la administración actual". En otras palabras, admiten que fue investigado por un discurso protegido por la Primera Enmienda.</p><p>Otros críticos de ICE han recibido un trato similar. El Wall Street Journal informa que la agencia "ha desplegado una red digital las 24 horas del día" que rastrea el discurso en línea para identificar más objetivos.</p><p>La campaña retaliatoria de ICE, advierten los abogados de Streever en la Fundación para los Derechos Individuales y de Expresión (FIRE), amenaza la libertad de criticar la conducta policial sin temor a ser arrestado. Hace cuatro décadas, la Corte Suprema describió esa capacidad como "una de las características principales por las que distinguimos una nación libre de un Estado policial".</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum es editor principal de la revista Reason. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: More than half of Gary residents without power 10 days after storm in historic outage
entries.summary: <p>As Lisa Bryant and her mom, Jackie, pulled up to the Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry, they thanked the pastor and volunteers loading their trunk with fresh groceries that would feed them for the next few days: bread, cheese, deli meats and canned goods.</p><p>The Bryants are among the thousands of residents in Gary who remain without power after severe storms tore through northwest Indiana last week, causing a historic outage that left much of the region in the dark.</p><p>“This will at least nourish us for a couple of days,” Bryant said as a box of food was loaded into her car.</p><p>Like many others, Bryant is unclear when power will be restored.</p><p>“It's completely dark,” said Bryant, 47. “It's been cool enough for us to raise the windows, but it's been terrible not knowing when our lights will turn on.”</p><p>Thursday marked 10 days since the majority of Gary residents have been without power after strong storms ripped through the city.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nipsco.com/outages/power-outages" target="_blank" >NIPSCO</a>, which serves all of Gary, said more than 22,000 of its 35,800 customers, or 61%, remained without power Thursday. The utility company said power would be fully restored in Gary by Tuesday, but Bryant said the company has repeatedly pushed back the restoration date. However, local efforts, like the food distribution event at the Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry, 5829 W. 15th Ave., are helping residents like the Bryants get through the blackout, which has also taken a financial toll.</p><p>Bryant said the outage has spoiled all of her refrigerated and frozen food, and she can’t afford a generator to keep her appliances running.</p><p>“Even if I could afford the generator, the person on the next street got their generator stolen off the porch,” she said. “If I do spend the money for a generator and somebody steals it, I'm still back in the same darkness.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-810000" name="image-810000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lisa Bryant looks over at Jackie Parker Bryant Thursday during a grocery and food handout at Gospel Truth Apostolic Ministry at 5829 W. 15th Ave. in Gary.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Pastor Valerie Clarke said the church distributes groceries at least once a month, but the need in the community has grown amid the ongoing power outages.</p><p>“The community is totally devastated,” Clarke said. “But while we don't have power, we're grateful that we still have our lives.”</p><p>Clarke said the church is doing what it can to help those in need.</p><p>“No one should have to go hungry,” she said.</p><p>Bryant said the outage has also cost her income. She works as a food service manager at a nearby school, but classes citywidehave been canceled until power is restored. </p><p>The Gary Community School Corporation did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>While Bryant has been without power, her parents have had to spend extra money to run a generator that keeps their medical equipment operating and their medications refrigerated.</p><p>Parker Bryant and her husband, Alan, both rely on CPAP machines to sleep, while Alan, who has diabetes, needs to keep his medication refrigerated.</p><p>“We’re retired. We don’t have money to spare,” said Parker Bryant, 75.</p><p>Businesses in Gary have also been hit hard by the outage.</p><p>Local restaurants, gas stations, grocery stores, banks, along with other private businesses are still without power. Many remained closed while others were operating in a limited capacity.</p><p>Saleh Mohamed, owner of the Clark gas station at 2295 Richard Gordon Hatcher Blvd., said he had to close the business for four days before he could get a generator.</p><p>He’s using two generators to power the business, but they’re only enough to keep the gas pumps, cash register and lights running.</p><p>“It’s unbelievable,” he said. “We thought it was going to be a day or two and we’d be good to go.”</p><p>Mohamed said that when the business reopened Sunday, they were overwhelmed by customers looking to fill up their cars or gas cans for generators. Business has since slowed, but he said the station is one of only a few in the area that remain open.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure a restoration timeline for businesses, as NIPSCO is prioritizing residential areas over businesses.</p><p>Hospitals have been restored, though, due to their critical need. Officials said they have been told that power for other businesses and residents could possibly be restored by Tuesday.</p><p>Mayor Eddie Melton acknowledged Wednesday how frustrating and difficult the outages have been for residents and said that a $100,000 donation from Hard Rock Casino Northern Indiana would support ongoing storm recovery efforts across the city.</p><p>“You have been patient, you have been been understanding and you’ve been frustrated with the delays, just like me and my family,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/19/gary-power-outage-deadly-storms" target="_blank" ><u>Melton said Wednesday</u></a>. “Progress is being made, power is actively being turned on. But many residents are still suffering without power.”</p><p>The funds will provide direct assistance to residents affected by the storm and help distribute critical supplies, including food, water, health and hygiene products, and cleaning and debris-removal materials.</p><p>Bryant said Gary residents were resilient, but after nine days without power, they had endured enough.</p><p>“Just turn the lights on,” Bryant pleaded. “That’s all I ask.”<br></p>
